articles.title: Children brave snipers and mortars to go to school near Yemen front line
articles.summary: In rare access to Taiz, the BBC World Service speaks to children, teachers and families affected by the war.

blocks.text: Image source, Liam Weir / BBC
Rafeef says the journey to school terrifies her, but she is determined to keep going
ByNawal Al-Maghafi
Reporting fromTaiz, Yemen
Every morning at 6am, 10-year-old Rafeef and her younger brother get ready for school, putting on their cream and brown uniforms.
She always looks forward to seeing her friends and learning about everything from maths to Arabic and Islamic studies. She can't wait to start studying English next year.
But for Rafeef, the journey to school involves far greater risks than crossing roads or missing the bus.

Her school in Taiz, south-western Yemen, stands on a mountain at the edge of a valley known as no-man's land - a heavily contested front line in the civil war between forces supporting Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, and the Iran-backed Houthis.
On one side of the school is government-held territory, on the other are Houthi sniper positions.
Rafeef's home is further down the mountain.
Every time she goes to school, she has to walk uphill with her back towards the snipers. "I'm afraid," she says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Rafeef's school is overlooked by Houthi positions on the mountains beyond the valley

blocks.text: Rafeef's school is overlooked by Houthi positions on the mountains beyond the valley
According to Unicef, roughly 3.2 million children in Yemen were out of school even before the war escalated last month.
It says thousands of children have been killed or maimed since the war began in 2014, while thousands more have been recruited by armed groups on both sides.
Yet despite the risks, Rafeef says she does not want to stop going because she loves seeing her friends and it is her only chance to be with them. She begins naming the children in her classroom.
Going to school is the only time Rafeef's parents let her go outside. They say they are keen for her to get an education and have the chance of a better life. Rafeef hopes to become a doctor.
'A mortar came out of nowhere'
Rafeef's family moved to Taiz from the coastal city of Hudaydah nine years ago, seeking safety when Houthis took control there.
But Taiz has also endured fighting.
Rafeef says that two years ago there was a mortar attack outside her new home.
"Everyone was out except for me and my brother. Then a mortar came out of nowhere… shrapnel blew through the door and into the house." Her arm was broken and there is still a scar where she was hit.

And in recent days the conflict has intensified. On Sunday the Houthis cut off a vital supply route linking Taiz to Aden, which meant they were able to effectively encircle Taiz. Control of that route has kept shifting.
Residents have told the BBC they are afraid the Houthis could seize the city at any moment.

Government forces have made gains in other areas this week, they say, retaking control of strategic points on the Bab al-Mandab Strait - a key shipping chokepoint - and launching an offensive to try to regain control of the capital, Sanaa.
Homes in Taiz are mostly scattered across the slopes, but many have been abandoned by families fleeing the fighting.
Twice, we try to visit the neighbourhood where Rafeef and her family live, but a community leader advises us it is too dangerous.
On the first occasion, residents of the neighbourhood tell us that three people have been shot by snipers. On the second, we are told of another shooting.
At Rafeef's school, one of the teachers, Abdel Raqeeb al-Obaidi, 45, takes us on to the rooftop to show us what he says are Houthi military camps, barracks and sniper positions in the mountains.
Standing on the rooftop, a Yemeni security adviser accompanying us suddenly tells us to go back inside. We are visible from these positions and could be shot, he says.
Abdel Raqeeb laughs, acknowledging the danger. He says the school has been fired on before.
"The situation may explode at any moment while we are sitting in class or sleeping or we are in school or we are out on the street. We do not know how our future is and how tomorrow is."
For Abdel Raqeeb, the risk has become routine. His familiarity with it is unsettling.

blocks.caption: A map of Yemen, showing the position of Sanaa in the west, Taiz in the south-west, and Aden on the south-west coast. The Bab al-Mandab Strait to the south-west tip of Yemen is also marked. The Red Sea is to the west of the country, and Saudi Arabia is to the north of Yemen.

blocks.text: Taiz has long been a major battleground in the country's devastating civil war. After ousting the government from the capital Sanaa in 2015, the Houthis attempted to also seize control of Taiz but were driven out of most of the city by local militiamen.
Seizing Taiz would give the Houthis full control over the country's north. Now, in their latest offensive, Houthis are making extensive use of drones alongside other weapons.
Sometimes civilians are collateral damage in the fighting.
Later that evening, we get a call from a hospital about a five minute drive away from the school. Two children have been badly injured by a mortar strike.
When we arrive at Al-Rawdah Hospital, we see a nurse standing outside the intensive care unit, holding a tiny pair of beige, rubber sandals that are splattered with blood.
They belonged to Ahmed, a three-year-old boy who we learn was killed when a mortar struck a mechanic's shop in the city.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The shoes a three-year-old boy, Ahmed, was wearing when he was hit by a mortar

blocks.text: The shoes a three-year-old boy, Ahmed, was wearing when he was hit by a mortar
Shrapnel in the heart
When I ask about the shoes, the nurse, Ikram Shamsan, begins to cry.
"What did this child or his family ever do wrong?" she asks.

Ahmed was killed when a piece of shrapnel pierced his heart, entering through his back. The boy had been with his father, who was getting his motorcycle tyre pumped up at the mechanic's shop. The father was unharmed.
A doctor tells us the father had intended to leave his son at home, but the boy cried because he wanted to come too.
As he takes his son's body from the hospital, the father asks how he will face the boy's mother.
Completing a simple errand turned into the worst day of their lives.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Amjad's mother does not know if he will survive after he was injured by shrapnel

blocks.text: Amjad's mother does not know if he will survive after he was injured by shrapnel
Another boy, 11-year-old Amjad, was also at the mechanic's shop. He and his brother worked there with their uncle, sending money to their family in their home village.
Shrapnel has struck Amjad in his lung and abdomen. When we reach him, he is in intensive care, struggling to breathe. No relatives are beside his bed.
His doctor describes his condition as critical and fears he could die within hours. He hopes his mother will arrive in time to say goodbye.
Amjad was admitted at about 20:00 that evening. His mother reaches him at around 06:00 the following morning, delayed by the eight-hour journey from the village.
She sits beside his bed and prays, trying to remain composed. Once outside the room, she falls to her knees and breaks down.
Doctors say his heart rate improves during her visit. They judge him stable enough for another operation.
He has since undergone that surgery, but remains critically ill.
"We're always terrified. It's devastating to see children killed," says nurse Shamsan. "We want peace and we want to be safe."
Additional reporting by Jasmin Dyer

articles.title: Sara Duterte denies Gracioso cash delivery allegations
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte rejected allegations by dismissed policeman Rodulfo Mondigo Gracioso Jr. that he delivered suitcases of cash to her and members of her family.

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte rejected allegations by dismissed policeman Rodulfo Mondigo Gracioso Jr. that he delivered suitcases of cash to her and members of her family.
Duterte said Gracioso’s sworn statement and media interviews falsely linked her to events that she neither committed nor had knowledge of or personally experienced.

“Mariin kong tinatanggi ang mga pahayag ni Rodulfo Mondigo Gracioso Jr. sa kaniyang sinumpaang salaysay at mga panayam sa media na iniuugnay ako sa mga pangyayaring hindi ko ginawa, hindi ko nalalaman, o hindi ko personal na naranasan,” Duterte said during a livestreamed press briefing on Tuesday, October 6.

(I strongly deny the statements made by Rodulfo Mondigo Gracioso Jr. in his sworn affidavit and media interviews linking me to events that I did not commit, was not aware of, or did not personally experience.)
The vice president said her camp would submit her affidavit to authorities on Thursday, October 8.

Gracioso has alleged that he delivered cash to Duterte, Davao City 1st District Rep. Paolo “Pulong” Duterte and former President Rodrigo Duterte upon the instructions of former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco.
Duterte disputes Gracioso’s claims
Duterte rejected Gracioso’s account that he fetched her from a private hangar in Pasay, drove her in a white Ford Savanna van and brought her to Diamond Hotel.
She said the Presidential Security Group handled her security from July 2016 to June 2022 and that her flights during that period were arranged through the PSG.
"Hindi kailanman nangyari na ako ay sinundo ni Gracioso sa isang private hangar sa Pasay, sumakay sa isang Ford Savanna White na artista van at hinatid sa Diamond Hotel," she said.
(It never happened that Gracioso picked me up at a private hangar in Pasay, where I boarded a white Ford Savana artist van and was taken to Diamond Hotel.)
She also said she did not own such a vehicle and that there were no records showing she visited Diamond Hotel.
Duterte questioned why she would need to speak with or thank Gracioso, saying she could communicate directly with Lord and his wife Rowena “Wen” Velasco.
She also denied that Royce Chocolate was her favorite, saying she seldom eats sweets because she is diabetic.
Duterte rejected Gracioso’s claim that former Davao City chief information officer Jefry Tupas was her personal aide who received cash on her behalf.
“Hindi ko katiwala, assistant, or personal staff si Tupas,” she said.
(Tupas is not my trustee, assistant, or personal staff.)

Duterte said she believed Gracioso included Tupas in his allegations because he mistook their friendship and Tupas’ attendance at her events as a sign that he was her subordinate. She also accused Gracioso of targeting Tupas because of homophobia.
She likewise denied owning a Hermes bag or a Patek Philippe watch.
Photos as rebuttal
Duterte presented photos of her activities to dispute Gracioso’s claims about her whereabouts in April 2019.
She said she was in Davao City for her mother’s birthday on April 14, followed by campaign rallies in Mati and Tagum on April 15, Digos on April 16, and Koronadal and Tacurong on April 17.
She said she spent April 18 to 20 at Island Buenavista before attending an Easter Egg Hunt in Davao City on April 21.
Her itinerary also showed trips to Cotabato City and Kidapawan on April 22, Malaybalay and Valencia on April 23, Puerto Princesa on April 24, and Bongao, Tawi-Tawi and Jolo, Sulu on April 25.
Duterte also disputed Gracioso’s claim that he went to her house, saying the property was too small to have the receiving area he described.
“Ang ibig sabihin lamang nito ay hindi nakapunta si Gracioso sa bahay namin dahil hindi niya alam kung anong itsura ng bahay namin,” she said.
(This simply means that Gracioso never went to our house because he did not know what our house looked like.)
She denied receiving vehicles or having an aide named “Kuya Tony.”
Duterte also denied knowing Ramil Madriaga, who identified himself as her former aide and bagman.
“Kung kunyaring totoo ang maleta na may P20 million na binigay kay Ramil Madriaga, sa bahay ko pa mismo, nakakapagtaka na hindi ito binanggit ni Madriaga,” she said.
(If the suitcase containing P20 million that was supposedly given to Ramil Madriaga at my house were indeed true, it is surprising that Madriaga did not mention it.)
She also rejected Gracioso’s claim that cash from Velasco was used to buy a motorcycle, saying she bought it in December 2017.
Velasco connection
Duterte said she believes Gracioso was among the men tasked by Rowena Velasco to monitor her husband.
“Paliwanag ni Lord, ang grupo ng mga lalaki ay ‘padala’ ni Wen na mga tagabantay upang mag-report sa kanya kung si Lord ay nambababae,” Duterte said.
“Ayon sa mga larawan ay naniniwala ako na si Gracioso ay isa sa mga taong tinutukoy ni Lord noon na tagabantay sa kanyang pangbababae,” she added.

Duterte said she met the Velascos during her father’s presidency, when Rowena introduced herself as a businesswoman close to San Miguel Corp. president Ramon Ang. She said Rowena also introduced her husband, who was then a politician in Marinduque.
NBI probes Gracioso's claims
Meanwhile, the National Bureau of Investigation continues to look into Gracioso’s allegations.
NBI Director Melvin Matibag said investigators are validating the claims through records and other means and are not relying on Gracioso’s lie detector test.

The NBI has found that two properties identified by Gracioso as “cash houses” are owned by the Velascos. Investigators are also checking corporate, tax and financial records involving properties and businesses linked to the couple.
Matibag said these records showed that some of Gracioso’s claims about the Velascos’ relationship and assets were consistent with available documents, although the investigation remains ongoing.
The Velascos, through their lawyers, have previously denied Gracioso’s allegations.

articles.title: Dismantling fixtures from vacated office an accepted practice in Senate, says Estrada's staff
articles.summary: Dismantling fixtures and other materials from a Senate office previously occupied by a senator is an established and accepted practice, the staff of Sen. Jinggoy Estrada said on Tuesday.

blocks.text: Published October 6, 2026 3:21pm
Dismantling fixtures and other materials from a Senate office previously occupied by a senator is an established and accepted practice, the staff of Sen. Jinggoy Estrada said on Tuesday.

Estrada's staff issued the statement after videos posted online showed the office of the Senate President Pro Tempore, previously occupied by Estrada, stripped bare of fixtures, tiles, and other amenities.
"It must also be emphasized that similar instances of dismantling fixtures and materials from a vacated senator's office have occurred in the recent past," the statement read.

"This is neither new nor unusual — it is an established and accepted practice within the institution, and singling out this particular transition for scrutiny is both unfair and misleading," it added.

The office said Atty. Racquel Mejia, Estrada's chief of staff, informed the incumbent Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente Sotto III, ahead of the October 5, 2026 deadline given to vacate, "that the fixtures, furnishings, and materials in the office would be brought along to the Senator's new office."

"Most of these items (e.g. floor tiles, glass panels, lighting fixtures, cabinets etc.) were acquired using personal funds, as the budget provided by the Senate was insufficient to cover all the expenses incurred," the statement read.

The statement said that reusing these materials in the new office reflects “prudence and efficiency, not controversy,” and noted that the matter has already been fully explained to the resident COA auditor.
Estrada also pointed out that when he first took over the office, he similarly found it completely bare, noting that this is an established practice in the Senate.

“It is also worth mentioning, in the spirit of full transparency, that the said vacated office, when it was turned over to Senator Estrada in 2022, was likewise bare, following this same long-standing practice. Standard practice ito sa Senado at hindi na dapat ikagulat pa o gawin pang isyu,” the statement read.
(This is standard practice in the Senate and should not come as a surprise or be turned into an issue.)
“It must also be emphasized that similar instances of dismantling fixtures andmaterials from a vacated senator's office have occurred in the recent past,” it added.
In a post on X, Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson refuted the claim that Estrada similarly moved into a bare and stripped office when it was turned over to him in 2022.

“I take exception to the statement pertaining to the state or condition of the same Pro Tempore office that I turned over to Sen. Estrada in 2022. Nothing was removed nor destroyed, precisely because government funds were used when I refurbished it when it was turned over to me,” Lacson said.
In June, Estrada was detained at the Quezon City jail after the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division ordered his arrest on non-bailable charges of plunder.
Since then, he has been unable to attend Senate hearings due to his ongoing detention. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: Hontiveros: China state-owned businesses remitted funds to Sara Duterte-linked Cale88
articles.summary: The National Security Council says it will look into the allegation which it 'takes seriously'

blocks.text: VEEP. Vice President Sara Duterte.
Inday Sara Duterte Facebook page
The National Security Council says it will look into the allegation which it 'takes seriously'

items: Senator Risa Hontiveros revealed that Cale88 Food Corporation, linked to Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, received significant remittances from Chinese state-owned firms during Duterte's impeachment trial.
The Chinese embassy denied the allegations, condemning them as political manipulation and asserting that they harm China-Philippines relations.
The National Security Council stated it would investigate the reported inflow of Chinese funds to Cale88, emphasizing the need for careful assessment of any national security implications.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Is a Philippine-based company with ties to Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio, receiving funds from Chinese state-owned firms?

During the continuation of Duterte’s impeachment trial on Tuesday, October 6, Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros disclosed that an investigation by her office showed that Cale88 Food Corporation received remittances from Chinese companies, including entities linked to China’s state-owned sector.

Among them are China National Township Enterprises (CNTE), which Hontiveros said operates under the supervision of the State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission of the State Council (SASAC).

SASAC is a ministerial-level institution under China’s State Council that oversees non-financial state-owned enterprises. Hontiveros said CNTE was previously under China’s Ministry of Agriculture before it came under SASAC.
Hontiveros also identified Beijing Zhenweifang Food Company, which she said also made remittances to Cale88.

Hontiveros said one of Beijing Zhenweifang Food Company’s major investors is Xinjiang Fruit Industry Group, which she described as a Chinese state-owned enterprise that “advances the interests of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).”

She also pointed to the company’s corporate governance structure, saying it includes CCP organizations, including a party committee, a Party Committee Organization Department, and 11 subordinate party branches.
Hontiveros further noted that the chairperson of Beijing Zhenweifang Food Company is allegedly a member of the district-level Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC).

“A US economic and security report showed that delegates to the CPPCC serve as proxies for CCP interests, and they frequently act as interlocutors with foreign government officials, businesses, and academic institutions,” Hontiveros said.
She also cited reports from Canada and Australia describing the CPPCC’s role in China’s United Front activities and raising concerns about its links to foreign influence operations.

blocks.caption: Hontiveros: China state-owned businesses remitted funds to Sara Duterte-linked Cale88

blocks.text: The disclosures came a day after Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura told the impeachment court that Cale88 received P319 million from China and Hong Kong, based on covered transaction reports (CTRs) and suspicious transaction reports (STRs).
Of the amount, P315.93 million came from mainland China, while P3.39 million came from Hong Kong.

Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV previously accused Carpio of receiving P319 million in cash remittances from China through Cale88. The company is listed in the Vice President’s Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) from 2022 to 2025.
The Chinese embassy in Manila denied the allegations.

“We strongly condemn and firmly oppose such malicious rhetoric and actions. We urge the relevant individuals in the Philippines to stop political manipulation and not to drag Philippine domestic politics into China-Philippines relations,” the embassy said in a statement.

“Attempts to achieve personal political gains by smearing and discrediting China and harming China’s interests and image are doomed to fail, and will ultimately undermine the interests of the Philippines and its people,” it added.
In a separate media briefing, House prosecutors raised concerns over Hontiveros’ allegations, saying these raise questions of possible constitutional violations by Duterte.
Prosecutor Terry Ridon said the House prosecution panel will discuss whether the information could be incorporated into its presentation on Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth.
“Mabigat na alegasyon ito, but we will discuss with the team kung maihahabol ba namin ito within the limited time and days that we have in the presentation of our evidence,” Ridon said.
(This is a serious allegation but we will discuss with the team if we can still do this within the limited time and days that we have in the presentation of our evidence.)

The National Security Council (NSC), for its part, said it would look into the reported inflow of Chinese funds to Cale88, saying it “takes seriously” the information presented during the impeachment proceedings.

“The NSC will look into the information presented and, as a matter of policy, continue to task the intelligence and investigative agencies and coordinate with relevant government institutions to assess the national security implications, if any, arising from the reported transactions,” National Security Adviser Eduardo Oban said in a statement.
Oban said the information presented at the trial remained subject to vetting through established legal processes.

He said that “the reported transactions and any credible information involving significant foreign financial flows that may bear upon the country’s national security warrants careful, in-depth, and responsible assessment.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Israeli ambassador to Australia says he hopes for return to ‘traditional friendship’ on October 7 anniversary eve
articles.summary:
Relations have soured between the two countries over a number of issues since 2023, but Hillel Newman says a ‘reset’ is possible

  • Get our

blocks.text: Israel’s ambassador to Australia says the third anniversary of October 7 is an opportunity for both countries to return to “traditional friendship”.

But, in the lead-up to commemorations on Wednesday marking Hamas’ terror attack, leaders of Australia’s Palestinian community say the federal government should do more to help the diaspora suffering since the war on Gaza.
Speaking ahead of the anniversary, Hillel Newman acknowledged relations had become “strained” between Australia and Israel but wanted to see improvement.

“We have challenges, but I have come with a lot of goodwill in order to try and make a positive change in the relationship, perhaps even reset the relationship and return both sides to the initial historical traditional friendship,” the Israeli ambassador told Guardian Australia.

“There have been issues between our two countries. We can have differences of opinion, but we should not allow differences of opinion to overshadow and overcrowd the overall relationship. We can understand if Australia has criticism of this issue or another.”

The comments come despite Israel’s foreign ministry publicly criticising foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, on social media in recent weeks, branding comments she made to the United Nations about settler violence in the West Bank a “blatant lie”.

It follows an earlier intervention into domestic Australian politics, where Israel urged Labor to soften criticism in a draft policy platform that condemned settler violence and a controversial death penalty law.

Since the 2023 attack – in which Hamas militants killed about 1,200 Israelis and 250 people were taken hostage, in what is considered the single deadliest day for Jewish people since the Holocaust – there has been a near breakdown in ties between the Israeli government and federal Labor.
Israel’s response to the attack and bombardment of Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians.

Australia has joined other countries in taking an increasingly stronger stance against Israel, including action alongside the UK, Canada and New Zealand to sanction Israeli politicians Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, accusing the two of inciting violence against Palestinians.
But the federal government last month stopped short of joining the UK and other partners in imposing a ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Relations deteriorated further when Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom was killed in a humanitarian convoy struck by Israeli drones in April 2024. Albanese and Wong slammed a decision by the Israel Defense Forces in August not to pursue criminal proceedings over Frankcom’s death.

Pressed on Israel’s failure to release audio from the strike, Newman stressed it was an issue for the Israeli military, but that his country remained open to any request for potential reparations for Frankcom’s family and remained in favour of continued discussions.

blocks.caption: Hillel Newman pictured outside Parliament House in Canberra on 20 August. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP

blocks.text: Wong has been working with the Frankcom family on an appropriate response to the decision not to press criminal charges.

She said in a statement that the Australian government had condemned the Israeli government’s decision not to pursue criminal proceedings against those responsible for killing Frankcom and her World Central Kitchen colleagues.
“The Australian government will not stop pressing Israel for justice for Zomi and her colleagues. We continue to engage closely with the Frankcom family on further action,” Wong said.

“7 October is a day of profound grief and remembrance. We mourn those who were killed in the Hamas terrorist attacks, including Australian Galit Carbone, and all those who have suffered from antisemitic violence around the world.”
The Australia Palestine Advocacy Network president, Nasser Mashni, said the impact from three years’ of war was measured in two places at once: Gaza and in the diaspora.
“In Australia, the impact is a quieter but a relentless erosion of our place in this country,” he said.
after newsletter promotion
“Underpinning every discussion that happens about ‘us’, but without ‘us’, is a nagging suggestion that we don’t belong, that we must prove we are Australian, and even human.
“This is the domestic footprint of genocide: protesting a demand for its end, and stopping Australia’s complicity in it, is more controversial than supporting it.”
In 2025, a UN commission found that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza, citing tens of thousands of civilian deaths and massive destruction. Israel strongly denies accusations of genocide.
The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, said Australians would reflect on the devastating toll of violence.
“The attacks on October 7 were condemned by the Greens at the time, as our party has a deep belief in peace and non-violence,” he said.
“It is that same core value that means we condemn the ongoing genocide in Gaza and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank.”

The cooler relations between Israel and Australia come against a backdrop of antisemitic attacks in Australia, as the nation prepares to face the first anniversary of the Bondi massacre on 14 December.
Fifteen people were killed by a father-son duo who opened fire on a Hanukkah celebration.
A royal commission sparked by the Bondi attack is due to release its final report on 18 December.
The Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-chief executive Alex Ryvchin said the October 7 attack and the “unsatisfactory responses” to it meant “troubled, uncertain times lie ahead for us all”.

“But if the jihadists thought mass terror at home and abroad would bring about some global capitulation by Israel and Jewish communities or that the majority of Australians would turn on their Jewish friends and neighbours, they have failed dismally,” he said.
The shadow defence minister, James Paterson, said the October 7 attack had changed Australia in “terrible ways” and culminated in the Bondi attack.
“Fixing this societal cancer will take years of sustained effort from the entire community, from the prime minister down,” he said.

articles.title: Keeping up with the Bolsonaros: Flávio’s surprise first-round election win heralds rise of a political dynasty
articles.summary: Four members of disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro’s family have been elected to office, most notably his wife and son Flávio, who won the first round of voting to be Brazil’s new…
articles.byline: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: The weekend’s elections in Brazil not only put Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the lead in the presidential race, but also underscored how far the former president has come in building a political dynasty.

As his far-right senator son heads into a runoff against the leftist incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a sweeping far-right victory in congressional races also secured seats for Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, two of his sons and one of his brothers.
Few in the family have spent much time working outside politics since the patriarch led the way four decades ago, but the offices they now hold have had a significant upgrade.

Former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro, 44, who divided her campaign with caring for her husband as he serves a sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup, ran for public office for the first time and was elected senator.

blocks.caption: Former first lady and senate candidate for the Liberal Party (PL), Michelle Bolsonaro, campaigning in Brasília.   Photograph: Sérgio Lima/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, 43, regarded as the most radical of the siblings – he ran his father’s social media accounts and was indicted by federal police for leading a so-called hate cabinet that spread fake news and attacks on opponents – was also elected senator for the first time.

His previous political career amounted to 25 years as a city councillor in Rio de Janeiro – starting at the age of 17, when his father put him up for a seat against his own mother, Rogéria Bolsonaro, who had divorced Jair. Carlos won. (Rogéria also ran last Sunday for a seat in the state legislature, still using the Bolsonaro surname, but lost.)

blocks.caption: From left, Jair, Michelle and Carlos Bolsonaro riding in an open car after Jair Bolsonaro’s swearing-in ceremony in 2019.   Photograph: André Penner/AP

blocks.text: The patriarch’s fourth son, Jair Renan Valle Bolsonaro, 28, who dropped his two middle names on the ballot to run simply as Jair Bolsonaro, jumped from city councillor to federal congressman.
Of Bolsonaro’s five children, only his 15-year-old daughter has never held political office.

Even the former president’s younger brother, Renato Bolsonaro, 62, nicknamed the “brother who can’t win” after losing seven consecutive elections for lower-level offices, was elected. He went from fewer than 10,000 votes in a mayoral race two years ago to 380,000 votes for congress.

During the campaign, Renato caused some friction within the family by saying that “Flávio is not Jair. He doesn’t draw crowds”. At the polls, however, Flávio ended up winning more votes than his father did in 2018 and 2022, although the result is seen by some as more of an anti-Lula vote than a strong preference for the senator.

The number of Bolsonaros in office could have been even higher had “son 03”, Eduardo Bolsonaro, 42, not abandoned his seat in congress and gone into self-imposed exile in the US, where for more than a year he has lobbied for what Lula and many others see as Donald Trump’s attempts to interfere in Brazil’s elections.

Although Michelle is the most recent member of the family to enter politics, it is she who is often considered to be the leading figure among the Bolsonaros. In a July poll, she was named the most powerful woman in Brazilian politics, well ahead of the current first lady, Janja Lula da Silva, in addition to a supreme court justice and many members of congress.

“She is a phenomenon,” said Camila Rocha, a researcher at the Brazilian Center for Analysis and Planning, who has interviewed voters and studied the Brazilian right for a decade. “Even Bolsonaro voters don’t like his sons very much, but many of them like Michelle, who is very charismatic.”

blocks.caption: Eduardo Bolsonaro with his father in São Paulo in June 2025. Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./Alamy

blocks.text: The daughter of a housewife and a retired bus driver from the metropolitan region around Brasília, Michelle was working as a parliamentary secretary for another politician when, at 25, she met Bolsonaro, then a 52-year-old congressman. She is his third wife.

When he took office as president in 2019, Michelle made history by becoming the first and only Brazilian first lady to deliver a speech at an inauguration. She did so in Brazilian Sign Language, which she had mastered while working as an interpreter at evangelical church services – her religiosity is seen as one of the main assets behind Bolsonaro’s close relationship with evangelical voters.

Despite playing by Bolsonaro’s party’s rules, Michelle was at the centre of one of the most contentious moments of Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign, when she said that she had been “humiliated”, “disrespected” and “mistreated” by the senator. Reports of friction between her and her stepsons are frequent. Given her popularity, Flávio had to apologise publicly – although Michelle accepted it, the two did not campaign together.

Polls suggested Bolsonaro supporters would have preferred the former first lady as the presidential candidate, but the patriarch opted for his eldest son, and gave her the senate mission instead. “That was the mission my husband entrusted to me, and I will represent him, God willing,” she said in August.
Michelle and Bolsonaro’s sons were also widely seen as helping secure victories for other far-right candidates from Bolsonaro’s party, which will have by far the largest bloc in the next congress.
“Although the family has been in politics for a long time, many voters still see the Bolsonaros as representing ‘renewal’ and an anti-system vote,” said Rocha.
“So, to change everything, these voters want to throw a ‘bomb’ that blows up congress and Lula. And that bomb is the Bolsonaro family,” she added.

articles.title: A medieval manuscript has confounded scholars for centuries. Have they been reading it wrong all this time?
articles.summary:
Researchers argue incorrect binding of Voynich manuscript radically changes ideas about its drawings and indecipherable text

It has been called the world’s most mysterious manuscript: a…

blocks.text: It has been called the world’s most mysterious manuscript: a medieval set of pages filled with botanical drawings, astronomical diagrams, pictures of nude women and indecipherable text. Claimed at various times to be a book in a lost language, a musical score, an instruction manual or just an elaborate hoax, the so-called Voynich manuscript’s true meaning has defied cryptographers and codebreakers for centuries.

Now, new research offers an explanation for why a scholarly consensus over this enduring puzzle has been so hard to come by: not only because its truth is so profoundly mysterious – but because everyone has been reading its pages in the wrong order.

In an article published in peer-reviewed journal Digital Medievalist, Colin Layfield and Lisa Fagin Davis argue that the manuscript’s folded sheets may have originally been piled on top of each other as “singulions” – like a stack of Christmas cards – but were mis-bound in a more typical “nested” arrangement at some point in the mid to late 15th century.

blocks.caption: A page from The Voynich manuscript. Photograph: Photo 12/Universal Images Group/Getty Images

blocks.text: While their finding does not immediately de-code the script, written in what has commonly become known as “Voynichese”, the authors say their finding radically changes our idea of the manuscript’s function.

“There are a lot of people who wanted the Voynich to have been created by one mad genius working in their attic in medieval London or wherever,” said Davis. “In fact, the evidence suggests we’re talking about a more communal object, perhaps a set of booklets through which information was passed down from one generation to the next – the ‘lone genius’ idea is kind of out of the door.”

The manuscript’s unknown provenance has piqued scholarly interest ever since it surfaced in book collectors’ records in the 17th century. When it was bought in 1912 by Wilfrid Voynich, a Polish revolutionary and book dealer with a shop on London’s Soho Square, it was thought to be a scientific diary written by the 13th-century polymath Roger Bacon. Others have credited the codex to Leonardo da Vinci.
Recent chemical analyses of the manuscript, which is held at Yale University, have carbon-dated its parchment to between 1404 and 1438, ruling out these famous authorships.

Some scholars have argued that the text of the Voynich Manuscript is nothing more than gibberish intended as a hoax or a forgery, though recent linguistic analysis has found it more likely that it is written in a natural, if yet unidentified, language.

In 2019, a biology research assistant at the University of Bristol, claimed that the manuscript was written in a “calligraphic proto-Romance” language, but the findings were later disputed, and the university subsequently removed a reference to the claims from its website.

For their article “Singulion Structure and the Voynich Manuscript”, Layfield and Davis used a numerical analysis tool to compare blocks of text and found that many of the attached pages scored highly for coherence even when there were many intervening pages, suggesting the manuscript had been mis-bound.

blocks.caption: A page from the Voynich manuscript, an illustrated codex hand-written in an unknown writing system. Photograph: GL Archive/Alamy

blocks.text: There were also visual clues suggesting the pages were supposed to be read in a different order. In the current binding, some illustrations of streams or pipes run into the gutter – the blank space along the inner margins where pages are bound – but don’t fully match with the pictures on the opposite page. “Once you treat them as loose pages stacked together, all these artistic anomalies suddenly join up”, said Layfield, a senior lecturer in information systems at the University of Malta.
“Our hypothesis fixes a lot of problems with the structure of the manuscripts in a really elegant way”, said Davis, an expert on medieval handwriting.

She said the only other known medieval manuscripts she has found preserved in a singulion arrangement were Qurans from north Africa, which were likely meant to be handed out as small booklets for instruction purposes.

“I think it’s likely we are looking similarly at an object that was made by a community that wanted to pass its knowledge forward,” said Davis, adding that her hypothesis was supported by paleographical analysis suggesting the manuscript was written by up to five different scribes.

blocks.caption: The quality control operator of the Spanish publishing outfit Siloe Luis Miguel works on cloning the illustrated codex hand-written manuscript Voynich in Burgos in 2016.  Photograph: César Manso/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Some of the drawings in the manuscript resemble the female reproductive system, while others hint at herbal lore and astrology. “When you put all of this together, it starts to feel like a book of women’s folk knowledge that’s being preserved,” she said. “But you cannot prove that yet.”
As to the mystery of the manuscript’s language, Davis said it wasn’t out of the question that there would have been other manuscripts written in Voynichese.

“The problem is that so few manuscripts have survived from the middle ages, because they weren’t bound. The irony is that whoever mis-bound this manuscript still did us a huge favour by ensuring its survival.”

articles.title: Canada: Quebec separatists return to power, promise new independence referendum
articles.summary: Parti Quebecois has won the provincial election, but fallen short of a majority. Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says he will seek another referendum on independence but not while US President Donald…

image.caption: The result returns Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s party to power for the first time in more than a decadeImage: Mathieu Belanger/REUTERS

blocks.text: In the Quebec's provincial election on Monday the separatist Parti Quebecois (PQ) came in the lead after promising another referendum on independence from Canada but fell short of a outright majority.
The PQ, led by 49-year-old Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, was on track to win nearly 60 of the 127 seats in the National Assembly, just short of the 64 needed for a majority.
However, their return to power after more than a decade comes with a caveat as the minority government will need support from opposition parties to pass legislation and survive confidence votes.
"Quebecers elected the Parti Quebecois asking it to work with the other parties, and I heard that message," the PQ leader said.
St-Pierre Plamondon says dreams of independent Quebec
The PQ's return to power also brings to forefront the issue of identity of Quebec's French-speakers, who make up 80% of the population, and comes with a promise of an independence referendum.
St-Pierre Plamondon said he envisioned Quebec as a country on its own and that a referendum would allow Quebecers to decide their own future.
"I continue to dream and visualize that country," St-Pierre Plamondon said in his victory speech. "That dream will be realized one day."

The jubilant leader, however, made it clear that the referendum would not take place while US President Donald Trump remains in office. He said the decision would need "an informed and calm debate" and could not be allowed to be "hijacked by the theatrics of an unpredictable president."

blocks.caption: Coalition Avenir Quebec leader Christine Fréchette conceded defeat, saying voters had made their choice and that she took full responsibility for the "difficult result"Image: Mathieu Belanger/REUTERS

blocks.text: Severing ties with British monarchy?
The PQ's victory does not necessarily signal majority support for independence.
While in the last referendum for independence in 1995, just 50.58% to stay in Canada, recent polls show support for sovereignty at around 30%.
"If Quebec becomes independent it would make us politically, economically and militarily vulnerable," 19-year-old Alexia Gomez, 19 told news agency AFP.
The Liberals and Conservatives have also voiced their opposition to an independence referendum, further complicating the PQ's path.
On the other hand, in a move more likely to find resonance among Quebecers, St-Pierre Plamondon's party has also pledged to reduce Quebec's ties to the British monarchy.
Meanwhile, Monday's result comes just two weeks before Alberta voters decide whether to support beginning the process toward a referendum on separating from Canada.
Could Alberta separatists tear Canada apart?

articles.title: Sara Duterte denies Gracioso’s claims, says he’s motivated by money
articles.summary: 'Ayon sa mga pahayag ni Gracioso, malinaw ang dalawang bagay. Ang motibo niya ay sama ng loob sa mga Velasco at pera,' Duterte says

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Vice President Sara Duterte on Tuesday, October 6, denied the claims of former cop Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. that she allegedly received millions of pesos stuffed in suitcases and cars.

“Sa tingin ko naman wala siyang galit sa akin… Motivated siya by money (I don’t think he has any personal anger toward me. He’s simply motivated by money),” the Vice President said during her press conference in Davao City.

In his eight-page affidavit, Gracioso alleged that he delivered millions of pesos to the Vice President when she was still the mayor of Davao City. The former cop alleged that there were similar incidents like this, almost 10 times, from 2018 to 2020.
Gracioso alleged that the money came from Duterte ally, former House speaker Lord Allan Velasco.
He also claimed that he gave Royce chocolates to the Vice President several times, while former Davao City information officer Jefry Tupas allegedly received the money on Duterte’s behalf.
Tupas has denied Gracioso’s claim in an affidavit submitted to the National Bureau of Investigation.

“My affidavit itself is strong enough to crush the untruths he shamelessly told, which were presented in a manner that insults basic human intelligence. Gracioso, brazen in his lies but weak in his ability to deceive, is an embarrassment to the institutions he claims to represent with pride — the Philippine National Police and the Philippine p,” Tupas said.

During the presser, Duterte shared screenshots of her recent conversation with Velasco, where the latter confirmed that Gracioso used to work for him as a security detail. The Philippine National Police has confirmed earlier that Gracioso used to be a cop and was previously assigned to Velasco.

In the conversation, Velasco said Gracioso handled the campaign for their party-list, Ang Pusong Pinoy, in Samar. He was given money for the campaign and promised to give 100,000 votes, but only delivered 4,000, said Velasco.

“Tapos humingi ng tulong pampaospital at panggamot. Ang alam ko, Ma’am, sabi ni Wen (wife), in-ask sa’ng hospital at mga reseta at sagutin namin lahat. Umayaw po ma’am at gusto padalhan siya ng pera,” the former speaker said.

(Then he asked for help with hospitalization and medication. From what I understand, Wen said, we asked for the hospital details and the prescription so we could pay for everything. But he refused and asked for money instead.)
For Duterte, she should not be caught in the middle of the conflict between Velasco and his former security detail.

“Ano man ang naging problema o hindi pagkakaunawaan nina Lord at Gracioso, hindi dapat ako idadamay sa kanilang personal na alitan sa pera. Hindi dapat gamitin ang aking pangalan sa paghihiganti, sa mga kasinungalingan, at pagpapalakas ng walang ebidensya na impeachment complaint, at sa paninira sa politika,” said the Vice President.

(Whatever happened between Lord and Gracioso, I should not be caught in the middle of their personal dispute over money. My name should not be used for revenge, lies, to bolster the evidence in my impeachment complaint, or for political attacks.)
“Ayon sa mga pahayag ni Gracioso, malinaw ang dalawang bagay. Ang motibo niya ay sama ng loob sa mga Velasco at pera,” she added.
(Based on Gracioso’s statements, two things are clear. His motive is personal anger toward the Velascos and money.)

blocks.caption: The Gracioso affidavit: Ex-cop claims he delivered millions to Sara Duterte

blocks.text: Duterte presented photos with her family – with time codes – to dispute the dates mentioned by Gracioso in his affidavit.
The Vice President also denied personally knowing former House appropriations chairperson Zaldy Co, who’s now a fugitive due to his flood control-related cases.

In the affidavit, Gracioso alleged that before the May 2019 elections, Velasco told them to pack money into about 20 balikbayan boxes and suitcases, which they delivered along with boxes of cigarettes and noodles. He alleged the money came from Co.
“Hindi ko personal na kilala si Zaldy [Co] at hindi ko siya kaibigan (I personally do not know Zaldy Co and I’m not his friend),” said Duterte. – Rappler.com

articles.title: NAPOLCOM probes police colonel over alleged abuse, misconduct
articles.summary: The National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM) on Tuesday said it is probing Police Colonel Froilan Uy over allegations of abuse of authority, oppression, and other forms of misconduct.

blocks.text: Published October 6, 2026 2:50pm
The National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM) on Tuesday said it is probing Police Colonel Froilan Uy over allegations of abuse of authority, oppression, and other forms of misconduct.

"Their recommendation is this be subjected to a pre-charge investigation for grave misconduct, grave abuse of authority, oppression, grave neglect of duty, disgraceful and immoral conduct and conduct unbecoming of a police officer," NAPOLCOM Commissioner Ralph Calinisan said in a press conference.
NAPOLCOM is also considering placing Uy under preventive suspension amid the investigation.
GMA News Online has reached out to the National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO) regarding Uy's side on the matter but it has yet to respond as of posting time.

Allegations against Uy were raised by several complainants including Erika Jane Colle and her partner Christopher Teodoro Batallier, their friend who covered his face during the press briefing, as well as Baliwag barangay chief Jaynor Reyes and his sister Mira. All of them participated in person during the Napolcom press conference regarding Uy's alleged transgressions.
According to Batallier and Colle, Uy and his supposed mistress sought their help to pawn the cop's vehicle for P150,000.
The civilian couple offered the vehicle to their friend.

The complainants said the vehicle was not redeemed after nearly a year, adding that the civilian couple's house was later subjected to gunfire after they demanded repayment. They also presented a documented conversation which they said showed Uy's partner allegedly ordering the shooting.
According to their friend, one of the complainants was about to expose Uy on a TV program, but the cop allegedly threatened to file a carjacking case against him.

Further, when the civilian couple tried to ask help from the barangay, Uy and his partner allegedly used their influence and filed trumped-up charges against the complainants in Taguig and Pasay, where the cop was previously assigned.

NAPOLCOM also launched a motu proprio investigation after being shown an old video allegedly showing Uy physically assaulting his partner. The commission said the PNP Anti-Cybercrime Group verified that the video was real and not AI-generated.
A 2022 police blotter also showed that the woman had reported Uy for alleged physical and financial abuse, according to NAPOLCOM.

Investigators also supposedly verified allegations that Uy's partner was using a Philippine National Police (PNP) vehicle and was being escorted by police officers. NAPOLCOM also identified three officers allegedly assigned to escort her. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Australian army soldier killed and five others injured in training exercise in the Northern Territory
articles.summary:
Australian defence force identifies soldier killed in a vehicle rollover near Darwin as Corporal Brendan Hannam

• Get our

blocks.text: Brendan Hannam has been named as the Australian soldier who died in a vehicle rollover during a training accident near Darwin on Monday. Five others were injured.

Chief of the army, Lt Gen Susan Coyle, confirmed two of the five others injured remained in hospital in a stable condition in Darwin, while the other three are currently in Robertson Barracks in a hospital ward being monitored.
The incident occurred at the Mount Bundey training area, around 100km south-east of Darwin in the Northern Territory.
Coyle said Hannam was a junior non-commissioned officer in the fifth/seventh battalion and is survived by his partner and two young children.

“He is a much beloved junior leader in our army. He has served and sacrificed on two operational tours to Afghanistan in 2019 under Operation High and also he trained Ukrainians with the British Armed Forces in the United Kingdom under Operation Kudu,” Coyle said.
Marles in a social media post on Tuesday afternoon said the defence force had “experienced a tragic loss of one of our finest soldiers” but did not provide further details.

“Australia’s service men and women do an exceptional job training and fighting for our country. This work in the defence of our nation carries risk. Our thoughts in this difficult time are with their family and friends,” he said.
“Defence is currently working with and supporting all the families in this difficult time.”
In a separate statement, prime minister Anthony Albanese – who is in Tuvalu for the pre-COP leaders’ meeting – also sent condolences.

“There are no safe or easy days for those who serve in our country’s name. This sad incident is a terrible reminder of what families take on when their loved one bravely puts on our nation’s uniform,” he said.
“Every loss and every incident is felt deeply by the broader Defence family, but by none more so than their mates who served alongside them. We think of them today and every day.”
The NT’s chief minister, Lia Finocchiaro, indicated in a press conference that the incident had occurred on Monday evening.
She said two people were evacuated by helicopter to Darwin around 7.30pm, with another three taken by plane around 9.30pm.
“Our sincerest condolences to the family of the young service personnel who lost their life yesterday,” Finocchiaro said.

“Our thoughts and prayers are with the family who are obviously devastated by this loss and of course the support of our entire community is there for all of our service personnel who will be feeling this loss immensely.”
The NT’s police commissioner, Martin Dole, said officers had been sent to the facility to “assist defence” in responding.
He also declined to provide further details but said police were “helping to investigate on behalf of the coroner”.
after newsletter promotion
“Next of kin has been notified. We request that the privacy of Defence members and families is respected at this time,” the department said.
The incident comes following several high-profile training accidents claiming the lives of ADF personnel.
Jack Fitzgibbon, the son of the former Labor defence minister Joel Fitzgibbon, died in 2024 during a parachute incident during a routine training activity in Sydney.
Three separate inquiries were launched after the death of Fitzgibbon: a Comcare inquiry led by the commonwealth’s WHS regulator; a New South Wales coronial inquiry; and an internal defence probe.
Lachlan Muddle, an experienced paratrooper, died in March after a mid-air collision with another trooper during training above a Jervis Bay airfield.
Following Muddle’s death, Marles said the Australia defence force had been provided with recommendations from investigations into the death of Fitzgibbon.
“In both that incident [2024] and this one, it is vital that investigations are as thorough as humanly possible so that every lesson is learned,” Marles said in March.
The federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said the Coalition was awaiting further updates from the government “at the appropriate time.”
“It’s another tragic reminder that our men and women warfighters put their lives on the line even when they are not on mission,” he said in a statement.

“We are also thinking of the five soldiers injured in this incident. We wish them a full and swift recovery, and our thoughts are with their families who will be supporting them through this very challenging time.”
Joel Fitzgibbon, in a social media post on Tuesday, sent condolences to those affected in the Mount Bundey incident.
“It’s an another reminder that training exercises are a preparation for war and are risky in and of themselves. Lest we forget.”

articles.title: Hontiveros claims some firms funding Cale88 are Chinese state-owned
articles.summary: Senator-Judge Risa Hontiveros on Tuesday claimed that some of the Chinese firms that funded Cale88 Foods Corporation, a company linked to lawyer Mans Carpio, husband of Vice President Sara Duterte,…

blocks.text: Published October 6, 2026 2:47pm

Senator-Judge Risa Hontiveros on Tuesday claimed that some of the Chinese firms that funded Cale88 Foods Corporation, a company linked to lawyer Mans Carpio, husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, were Chinese state-owned enterprises.

Hontiveros made the allegation during her interjection on the 34th day of the impeachment trial, as she asked questions to Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura, a witness presented by the House prosecution panel.

The senator-judge said her office looked into the Chinese companies mentioned during Monday’s trial and found that some of those that sent money to Cale88 are Chinese state-owned enterprises that may be “advancing the interests of the Chinese Communist Party.”

“Isa na po doon ‘yung pinakitang China National Township Enterprises. Base po sa research ng opisina ko, dating ‘directly under the Ministry of Agriculture’ sa China, at naging isang, ‘large state-owned agricultural enterprise under the supervision of the State-Owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission of the State Council,’” Hontiveros said.

(One of these is the China National Township Enterprises. Based on my office’s research, it was formerly ‘directly under the Ministry of Agriculture’ in China and became a ‘large state-owned agricultural enterprise under the supervision of the State-Owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission of the State Council.’)

“At sa public profiles po ng China National Township Enterprises na ‘yun, binibida ng kumpanya na sila daw ay, ‘committed to serving the implementation of the country's Belt and Road Initiative and foreign policy,’” she added.

(And in the public profiles of China National Township Enterprises, the company highlights that it is ‘committed to serving the implementation of the country's Belt and Road Initiative and foreign policy.’)
Hontiveros said that another firm, Beijing Zhenweifang Food Company, is supposedly owned by the Xinjiang Fruit Industry Group, as stated in the company’s own materials.

“Kumpirmado din po itong Xinjiang Fruit ay Series A investor sa Beijing Zhenweifang. Mayroon ding strategic cooperation agreement itong dalawang kumpanya — ’yung Beijing at saka ‘yung Xinjiang mula pa 2019,” she said.

(It’s also confirmed that Xinjiang Fruit is a Series A investor in Beijing Zhenweifang. The two companies—the Beijing Zhenweifang and the Xinjiang Fruit—also have a strategic cooperation agreement since 2019.)

“Itong Xinjiang Fruit Industry Group ay hindi ordinaryong kumpanya (is not an ordinary company). It's a Chinese state-owned enterprise. It advances the interests of the Chinese Communist Party,” she continued.
Hontiveros then asked Buenaventura if the AMLC looked into such linkages.
The AMLC official, in response, said that he could not give a definite answer on the matter.

“Your Honor, apologies po. At this point po, ‘yung na-cover po nung subpoena is only on the records. Apology po hindi po 'ko makakatulong sa tanong po ninyo, but I'm unable to answer that po at this point,” Buenaventura said.
(Your Honor, apologies. At this point, what was covered in the subpoena was only the records. Apologies I can’t help answer your question at this point.)
Hontiveros further asked the witness if, as head of the AMLC Secretariat, he would consider such transactions a cause for concern.
“Your Honor, I note po the… I have to review po ‘yung binanggit niyo po. Hindi ko po nakuha lahat po, Your Honor. But we'll take note naman po ‘yung nabanggit po ninyo,” Buenaventura answered.
(Your Honor, I have to review what you mentioned. I didn't get it all, Your Honor. But we'll take note of what you mentioned.)
During the trial on Monday, Buenaventura confirmed that Cale88 Foods Corporation received P319 million from China and Hong Kong.
Of the amount, it was indicated in the table presented that P315.93 million came from Mainland China, while P3.39 million was from the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of China.

The Chinese Embassy in Manila branded the allegations that China has funneled funds to a political faction in the Philippines as a "false narrative," calling them "malicious rhetoric and actions.” — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Sara Duterte open to lie detector test, dares Gracioso to show results to public
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Tuesday said she is open to undergoing a lie detector test amid claims that she received suitcases containing cash, as long as dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.…

blocks.text: Published October 6, 2026 2:46pm

Vice President Sara Duterte on Tuesday said she is open to undergoing a lie detector test amid claims that she received suitcases containing cash, as long as dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. will reveal his results to the public.
“Wala akong problema sa lie detector test pero ipakita muna nila ‘yung public na lie detector test ni Gracioso,” Duterte said in a press briefing.
(I have no problem with a lie detector test, but they should first show the public the lie detector test of Gracioso.)
“Kasi ang nagke-claim lang naman na pumasa siya sa lie detector test is si Gracioso mismo,” she added.
(Because the only one claiming that he passed the lie detector test is Gracioso himself.)

Gracioso previously alleged that he delivered cash to the vice president, Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo Duterte, and former President Rodrigo Duterte on former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco’s instructions.
Prior to the issuance of his affidavit, National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag said Gracioso underwent a lie detector test.
He added that Gracioso passed 99% of that test.
After his affidavit, Gracioso took a second lie detector test with the NBI.
Velasco’s camp previously said the allegations against him had “no basis.”
Affidavit
The Vice President on Tuesday again denied claims made by Gracioso and read her affidavit answering his allegations, which she said her camp will submit to authorities on Thursday, October 8.

“Mariin kong tinatanggi ang mga pahayag ni Rodulfo Mondigo Gracioso Jr. sa kanyang sinumpaang salaysay at mga panayam sa media na inuugnay ako sa mga pangyayaring hindi ko ginawa, hindi ko nalalaman, o hindi ko personal na naranasan,” she said in a press briefing.

(I strongly deny the statements made by Rodulfo Mondigo Gracioso Jr. in his sworn affidavit and media interviews linking me to events that I did not commit, did not know about, or did not personally experience.)
Amid photos shown by Gracioso with the vice president, Duterte said that Gracioso cannot directly go to her due to the security of the Presidential Security Group (PSG).
She said that from July 2016 to June 2022, the PSG served as her security personnel.
“Hindi kailanman nangyari na ako ay sinundo ni Gracioso sa isang private hangar sa Pasay, sumakay sa isang Ford Savanna White na artista van at hinatid sa Diamond Hotel,” she said.
(Never was I fetched by Gracioso at a private hangar in Pasay, [never did I] ride a Ford Savanna White which is an artista van and [never was I] was brought to Diamond Hotel.)
Duterte also denied that former Davao City chief information officer Jefry Tupas, who Gracioso claimed received cash on her behalf, was her personal aide.

“Hindi ko katiwala, assistant, or personal staff si Tupas. Naniniwala ako na kaya si Tupas ang pinili ni Gracioso na isali sa kasinungalingan ay dahil akala ni Gracioso na si Tupas ay isang sunod-sunodan o lackey na bakla dahil nakikita niya na magkaibigan kami at uma-attend siya sa mga events ko,” she said.

(Tupas is not my caretaker, assistant, or personal staff. I believe Gracioso chose to include Tupas in the lies because Gracioso thought that Tupas was a follower or gay lackey because he saw that we were friends and that he attended my events.) —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Buckingham Palace says it will not fund Andrew’s legal action against police
articles.summary:
Former Duke of York is attempting to quash search warrants that led to his arrest in February

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been warned not to use the king’s private money to fund his legal…

blocks.text: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been warned not to use the king’s private money to fund his legal action against Thames Valley police.
The former Duke of York is attempting to quash search warrants that led to his arrest, with a private high court hearing due to take place on Thursday.

Mountbatten-Windsor receives an annual stipend – the amount of which has not been disclosed – provided by King Charles from his private funds, but a palace source told reporters it had been made clear this should not be used to fund the judicial review.
Mountbatten-Windsor’s legal defence was a matter for him and his lawyers, and Buckingham Palace had no role in determining its strategy or actions, the source is reported to have said.

The late queen’s second son was arrested on his 66th birthday earlier this year on suspicion of misconduct in public office, after allegations he had shared sensitive information with Jeffrey Epstein during his time as the UK’s trade envoy.
The Telegraph previously reported that Mountbatten-Windsor had been granted permission to challenge whether Thames Valley police acted lawfully over the searches relating to his arrest in February.
A judge at the Old Bailey issued warrants that allowed police to raid his residence on the Sandringham estate and his former Windsor home, Royal Lodge.
On Monday, a judicial spokesperson confirmed a hearing in Mountbatten-Windsor’s legal claim is due to take place at 2pm on Thursday at the high court, before Mr Justice Hilliard.
When Andrew was arrested on 19 February, the king issued a written statement saying “the law must take its course”.
The former duke, who now lives on the king’s private Sandringham estate in Norfolk, was interviewed under caution before being released under investigation.
Police began their searches of the properties on the same day, with the force confirming on 24 February that they had ended.
The judicial spokesperson said the hearing would concern an attempt by Thames Valley police to restrict access to court documents, with the hearing to begin in private.
It is not known whether Andrew will attend the hearing.

A Thames Valley police spokesperson said: “Whilst our investigation into misconduct in public office continues, we are engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the central criminal court.
“As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further.”

articles.title: Badenoch calls for UK ‘Iron Dome’ missile defence system - UK politics live
articles.summary:
Conservatives plan ‘new integrated air and missile defence system to protect Britain from attack – in essence, a British “Iron Dome”’

Q: You are going to cut inheritance…

blocks.text: Badenoch does not accept claims £10bn not enough to fund missile defence
Jon Kay is interviewing Badenoch.
He puts it to her that the UK would need a very different missile defence system from Israel. Israel is under threat from short-range missiles, he says.
Badenoch says it is not just missiles that threaten the UK; drones are a threat too.
Q: Would £10bn be enough to pay for it?
Badenoch says it can be done. The £10bn would be spent over 10 years, she says. She says the UK needs to be protected.
Key events

12m agoBadenoch says Penny Mordaunt was 'fantastic MP' - but rules out special treatment for ex-MPs in candidate selection
18m agoBadenoch won't say whether speech tomorrow will include plan to cut inheritance tax
20m agoBadenoch does not accept claims £10bn not enough to fund missile defence
25m agoBadenoch pays tribute to Jeffrey Archer, saying he sent her supportive text hours before he died
29m agoLib Dems say Tories would only be able to get 'Patchwork Dome' for £10bn
33m agoWhat Tories are saying about how their proposed 'Britannia Shield' would work
40m agoPolitics Badenoch calls for UK ‘Iron Dome’ missile defence system

blocks.text: Badenoch claims 'we haven't called it Iron Dome' - despite Tories using phrase in their press release
Q: You say your Iron Dome will protect the whole of the UK, and bases abroad. But Sir Richard Barrons, the former general, has said that a proper air defence like this would cost up to £100bn.
Badenoch says Barrons is referring to an Israel-style Iron Dome.
She says she is referring to something different. She says the UK should be able to defend itself from, for example, someone on a boat firing a drone at the system.
Q: But it is nothing like Israel’s Iron Dome. It is a gimmick, isn’t it?
Badenoch replied:
double quotation markIt’s not going to be exactly like the Irone Dome. We haven’t called it an Iron Dome.
But, in fact, they did. This is what they sent out to journalists yesterday.

blocks.caption: Press release Photograph: Conservative party

blocks.text: Badenoch is on Times Radio now. She is being interviewed by Kate McCann.
Asked when she would raise defence spending to 3.5% of GDP, Badenoch says she has a plan to get to 3%. But she is not in government.
Q: But you say there might be an election soon?
Badenoch says the 3.5% is a Nato target.
She says she is not in government, and she implies it is unreasonable for McCann to expect her to set out a path to 3.5% when she is not in government.
Badenoch says Penny Mordaunt was 'fantastic MP' - but rules out special treatment for ex-MPs in candidate selection
Q: Would you like to see Penny Mordaunt selected as a Tory candidate?

(At the weekend Mordaunt, the former cabinet minister who lost her seat at the election, revealed she has been approved for the candidates list, which means she can apply to be a candidate in a Tory seat.)
Badenoch says it is not up to her to decide; local parties choose their candidates, she says.
She says she wants “serious people” committed to public service as MPs.
Q: Do you want to see her selected?
Badenoch says Mordaunt was a “fantastic MP”. She says she was sorry she lost her seat, and is glad she wants to stand again.
But former MPs won’t get special treatment when candidates are being selected, she says. She says she wants candidate selection to be a “meritocracy”.
Badenoch won't say whether speech tomorrow will include plan to cut inheritance tax
Q: You are going to cut inheritance tax, aren’t you?
Badenoch says everyone knows she would like to do that. She has said that before.
But she won’t announce that unless she has found the money to pay for it.
Q: Will you have found the money by the time you give your speech tomorrow?
Badenoch tells Kay he will have to wait.
Badenoch pays tribute to Jeffrey Archer, saying he sent her supportive text hours before he died
Kemi Badenoch is on BBC Breakfast.
They start by asking about the death of Jeffrey Archer, and Badenoch says she got a message from him only yesterday morning. He said: “Great outfit, great speech, no need to reply.”
Badenoch says Archer was “a great communicator” and a “great storyteller”, and someone who believed in Conservatism.
Here is our story about his death.
Lib Dems say Tories would only be able to get 'Patchwork Dome' for £10bn

The Liberal Democrats have dismissed the Tory plan for a “Britannia Shield” as “Truss-style fantasy economics”. They say the Conservatives would only get a “Patchwork Dome” with the £10bn they plan to spend on the project.
James MacCleary, the Lib Dem defence spokesperson, said:

double quotation markOnce again the Conservatives are indulging in Truss-style fantasy economics. £10bn would not even touch the sides for a complete UK-wide ‘Iron Dome’. They either need to review their dodgy sums or come clean about which parts of the country their Patchwork Dome wouldn’t cover. Let’s not forget this is the party that hollowed out our armed forces for a decade, and whose disgraceful plan to fill the defence-spending black hole is based on targeted cuts to the poorest and most vulnerable children. You do not make Britain safer by pushing families into poverty.
What Tories are saying about how their proposed 'Britannia Shield' would work
This is what the Conservatives are saying about why the UK needs a “Britannia Shield” (their name for what they describe as a version of the “Iron Dome”), and who it would work.

double quotation markThe announcement comes as the threat of missile and drone attack against Britain and our allies continues to grow. Russia bombards Ukraine daily with ever more advanced drones and missiles, and they were behind a drone attack on Leipzig airport in August. Drones launched by Iranian proxies have hit our RAF base in Cyprus, and when Iran fired missiles at the Chagos islands earlier this year, it was the US who stepped in to launch interceptors. Nato allies, especially in the Baltic States, are suffering ever greater numbers of drone incursions and western intelligence agencies have warned that Russia could attack a Nato country by 2030. We live in an increasingly dangerous and unpredictable world, where threats to the UK and our allies are growing in scale and complexity, yet Britain remains dangerously exposed. A report in November 2025 by the defence select committee warned that, compared to European allies investing heavily in integrated air and missile defence, the UK has “next to nothing”. The Conservatives will close this dangerous capability gap by committing up to £10 billion over ten years. We will deliver a minimal deployable capability within our first term in office, with the remaining investment focused on expanding and strengthening the system over time. Britannia Shield will have three key components: SENSE: New advanced radar systems, to detect incoming missiles and drones. DECIDE: Upgraded command and control systems to integrate information from across Britain’s defences and rapidly identify the most effective response. EFFECT: New interceptor missiles, counter-drone capabilities, and significantly larger missile stockpiles to defeat incoming threats.
Politics Badenoch calls for UK ‘Iron Dome’ missile defence system

Good morning. Kemi Badenoch is doing a round of interviews this morning at the Conservative conference, and she will be talking about her plans for the UK to have its own version of Israel’s “Iron Dome” missile defence system. That phrase is not just journalists’ hype; it has come from the first line of the party’s press release, which says the party has plans for a “new integrated air and missile defence system to protect Britain from attack – in essence, a British ‘Iron Dome’.”
Here is our story by Jessica Elgot and Dan Sabbagh.
And this is what Badenoch is saying about it.

double quotation markThe first duty of government is to defend the country and keep people safe. Labour are failing that basic test. The world will not wait for Britain to get ready. War has returned to Europe. Missiles and drones are transforming warfare in the Middle East. Cheap weapons can now threaten cities, military bases and critical infrastructure in ways that would have sounded like science fiction a generation ago. If a missile or drone is launched at Britain, we do not get a second chance to wish we had prepared.

The Tories say their plan would cost £1bn a year over 10 years, and that the money would come from the plan they announced last month to raise defence spending by £10bn a year. Almost half the money for this would come from cuts to housing benefit.
Here is the agenda for the day.
7.30am: Kemi Badenoch begins a round of media interviews, starting with BBC Breakfast.

9.45am: The morning session of the Conservative party conference opens, with speeches from Katie Lam, the shadow housing secretary, then Laura Trott, the shadow education secretary (at 10.30am) and Rebecca Paul, the shadow culture secretary (at noon).

2pm: The afternoon session starts, with speeches from Alex Burghart, the deputy leader, Tom Tugendhat, the shadow foreign secretary, James Cartlidge, the shadow defence secretary, and Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.
