France has long had underlying fiscal problems. Since President Emmanuel Macron came to office in May 2017, public spending has climbed while he has brought in deep tax cuts. As a result, the country's national debt has increased by well over €1 trillion ($1.12 trillion).

France's debt-to-GDP ratio now stands at almost 118%. It consistently posts unbalanced budgets. Its annual budget deficit is now regularly more than 5%, above the 3.4% rate when Macron came to office.

For many investors, wider concerns over low eurozone growth levels and surging energy prices have contributed to a renewed focus on France, with many retreating to perceived safer options, such as German government debt.
The difference between French and German government 10-year debt yields reached their highest level since the eurozone debt crisis last week, a closely-watched measure of EU financial stability.
What can the ECB do?

The resulting pressure on the euro and on other government bond markets, including Italy's, means there are calls for the European Central Bank (ECB) to take action to prevent concern over France turning into panic.
Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid said in a note on Monday that at one point last week, the spread between German and French bonds had become so wide that a "mini-panic" was at hand.
"The big question is whether this is the start of a new euro sovereign crisis or whether markets have already overshot," he said.

blocks.caption: There is pressure on the European Central Bank to take actionImage: Jana Rodenbusch/REUTERS

blocks.text: Ricardo Amaro said the situation presents a challenge for the ECB because it needs to act without making things worse. "Sounding too hawkish would also add to pressure on France's bond yields, which became an important driver of euro weakness," he added.
He expects policymakers to continue monitoring currency developments between the US dollar and the euro, but to stop short of trying to influence the market for now.
What is at stake?

Uncertainty abounds due to both political and economic pressures. France has been beset by political crises in recent years, where passing annual budgets has become a major test of government stability.

Although the 2027 budget has been agreed, with reforms aimed at reducing the deficit, the right-wing National Rally remains well-placed ahead of the 2027 presidential election, in which Marine Le Pen is likely to be the lead candidate.

Concerns over French economic policy in the event of Le Pen winning the presidency are spooking investors, similar to how the rise of the populist AfD in Germany has raised questions over the future direction of the bloc's key economy.

Much of the political instability has been driven by voter anger over the high cost of living. In Spain, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has just called a snap election after measures to deal with the country's housing crisis were voted down in parliament.

blocks.caption: Political crises in France and Spain are fuelled by economic issuesImage: Cheng Min/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: Amaro says a weakening euro could compound the underlying problem of inflation.
"Sharper euro weakness would reinforce the inflationary shock at a time when inflation is already expected to stay high into 2027," he said.

A weaker euro would increase the cost of imported goods, particularly those that are priced in US dollars. Global commodities such as oil and gas are priced in dollars, meaning soaring energy prices would likely rise further, as would US imports.
The next financial crisis?

With memories of the sovereign debt crisis that afflicted the EU in the early 2010s still fresh, many observers are beginning to wonder if the moves on French debt could be indicative of a new crisis in the eurozone.
Some, such as Geoffrey Yu, a senior strategist with BNY, believes such concerns are misplaced. "Comparisons to 2012 are well off the mark," he said.

However, Amaro says the fact that further interest rate hikes are expected from the ECB this year, combined with the worsening inflation outlook, makes this a situation which needs to be managed and monitored very carefully.

"Euro weakness shouldn't be interpreted as an isolated development," he says. "If triggered by growing concerns about France's fiscal outlook, then the ECB would certainly want to thread that carefully given risks for the eurozone."

articles.title: Military aircraft with 32 people on board crashes in southern Nigeria
articles.summary: Rescue teams are searching the crash site after the military aircraft went down in southern Nigeria. The fate of those on board remains unclear.

image.caption: The plane involved in the crash is similar to the one in the picture (FILE: August 10, 2026)Image: Steven Mohr/SNS/picture alliance

blocks.text: A military aircraft carrying 25 passengers and seven crew members crashed in southern Nigeria, authorities said on Monday.
Nigerian President Bola Tinubu later said all 32 people on the plane had died in the crash.
The aircraft was on a routine mission to Lagos, Nigeria's economic hub, when it crashed in the Igbokoda area of Ondo state, Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo said in a statement.
Wreckage located
Keyamo said the aircraft disappeared from radar at around 9 a.m. local time (7:00 a.m. GMT) and was later found to have crashed about halfway through its journey from Edo state to Lagos.
He said the wreckage had been located near a naval base.
The Nigerian Air Force identified the aircraft as an ATR-42 and said an immediate search and rescue operation had been launched.
A video circulating on social media showed a small crowd gathered near a river as rescuers searched the area by boat.
Locals told AP news agency about what they had heard and seen.
"The plane cleared some trees. We found some body parts, some clothes and shoes," one of the locals said.

articles.title: Iran poised to exploit security vacuum as US leaves Iraq
articles.summary: The end of the US military mission in Iraq leaves the Kurdistan region facing a severe security vacuum. As Erbil grapples with deep internal divisions, Tehran is well positioned to make strategic…

image.caption: Iraqis last week celebrated the departure of final US forces after more than two decades of conflictImage: Ahmad Al-Rubaye/AFP

blocks.text: The end of the US military mission in Iraq has created a dangerous security vacuum for the semi-autonomous Kurdish region.
Politicians in Baghdad celebrated the withdrawal, with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi officially declaring October 1 a "Day of Sovereignty and Independence."
Tehran, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), and Iranian-backed Shiite militias also cheered the move.
But in Erbil, the capital of Iraq's Kurdish region, the mood is markedly more anxious.

Having relied on Washington's protection for two decades, the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI) now faces intertwined crises, including mounting pressure from Baghdad to centralize power and escalating military threats from its neighbors, most notably Iran.
Why Iraq can't escape the US and Iran
A strategy of containment

The immediate threat to the Kurdistan region isn't a full-scale military invasion, but rather a slow, calculated chipping away of its autonomy, said Hesam Dastpish, a Middle East analyst based in Brussels.
He describes Tehran's overarching strategy toward Erbil as hostile and heavily focused on containment.
The Islamic Republic ultimately wants to strip the KRI of its political clout, reducing it to a purely administrative body, the expert stressed.

"Tehran's goal is to turn the Kurdistan region into an institution with absolutely no room to maneuver," Dastpish told DW, pointing to Iran's repeated strikes in the region, supposedly targeting camps of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups.
Salahuddin Khadiw, a political analyst based in Mahabad in Iran's Kurdish region, said that neighboring states don't necessarily want to wipe out Kurdish autonomy completely.
Instead, he underscored, Tehran envisions a "controlled and weak" Kurdistan.

By dealing separately with the rival power centers in Erbil and Sulaymaniyah, he argued, Iran has maintained influence across the KRI while seeking to prevent any single Kurdish authority from emerging as a dominant power on its western border.
Internal fragmentation remains a fatal flaw
Despite the external challenges, the Iraqi Kurdish region's most critical vulnerability comes from within.
The legacy of the 1990s civil war lives on through the deeply entrenched rivalry between the two main ruling factions: the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK).

Hiwa Mahmoud Osman, an analyst on Iraqi and Kurdish affairs in the Middle East, pointed out that Tehran leans heavily on this internal friction. "Iran has spent decades mastering political influence inside Iraq," he told DW. "The Kurds' biggest hurdle is their own fragmentation. Without a united front, foreign powers simply have more room to operate."
What will the US troop withdrawal from Iraq mean for Kurds?

Ardeshir Pashang, a Middle East researcher in Tehran, warned that if Kurdish leaders fail to patch up their political quarrels, this disunity could ultimately lead to the collapse of the Kurdistan region as a political entity.
The opposition dilemma
A particularly thorny issue is the presence of Iranian Kurdish opposition outfits taking refuge in the KRI.
These groups, which have historically clashed with Iranian state forces, are now under immense pressure to disarm and relocate.
Their presence provides Iran with a convenient pretext to launch drone and missile strikes across the border, said Dastpish.
But he doesn't expect Erbil to offer "total surrender," as maintaining a balance with these groups is crucial for the KRI's domestic legitimacy and foreign relations.
Kasra Gharadaghi, a political science researcher based in Florida, argues that these groups are now more vulnerable than ever.

If Iran was able to strike their sanctuaries while US forces were still fully deployed — culminating in a 2023 border security pact between Baghdad and Tehran — Erbil's leverage is now practically non-existent, giving Tehran significantly more power to force concessions, he said.
Iranian Kurds in Iraq face war fears, exile
Dollar diplomacy is America's hidden weapon

While American troops may have left, Washington's leverage in Iraq has not entirely disappeared. It has simply transitioned toward global financial networks. Gharadaghi describes this as a "realignment of power," where the US, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia act as natural counterweights to Iran's growing reach.

Osman echoed this view, highlighting Iraq's deep financial reliance on the US dollar. This economic tether allows the US Treasury to indirectly influence Baghdad's internal affairs, right down to ensuring salaries are paid to KRI civil servants.
Khadiw similarly characterizes this strategic pivot as America transitioning from a "military balancer" to a "powerful economic observer."

But as internal and external pressures mount, the analysts said, Iraq's Kurdish region may have little choice but to heal its internal divides and present a united front to preserve its autonomy and limit Iran's strategic gains in the region.

articles.title: Trust in the German Constitutional Court is eroding — how can this be stopped?
articles.summary: Germany's top court, which turned 75 this year, is losing the population's trust, surveys show. Some say reforms in the way it picks candidates would help, to also accept candidates nominated by the…

image.caption: The Federal Constitutional Court is Germany's supreme court, based in KarlsruheImage: Bernd Weißbrod/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Federal Constitutional Court — Germany's equivalent of the US Supreme Court — still enjoys the most trust among the population of any branch of government, but that trust is slipping, according to recent surveys.

A new survey by the pollsters YouGov, commissioned to mark the 75th anniversary of the founding of the court, found that about two-thirds (66%) of Germans trust the Federal Constitutional Court. This was significantly more than the other major branches of the country's government system: The Bundesrat, the upper house of the German parliament, scored 47%, the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag 38%, and the Federal Government itself 29%.
But other surveys show those figures were significantly higher just a few years ago: One study from 2025 by the Allensbach Institute found that trust in the court was as high as 81% in 2021.

Exactly why this has happened remains a matter of conjecture: As a possible explanation, some analysts have pointed to the decisions the court made to allow the government to curtail certain freedoms during the COVID-19 pandemic — which precipitated many protests.
That period also saw an overall drop in trust in all the branches of government, and this decision, some argued, showed that the court was not an independent arbiter after all.

blocks.caption: President Frank-Walter Steinmeier spoke about the importance of the Constitutional Court during the anniversary ceremonyImage: Uli Deck/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Can the Constitutional Court be 'too political?'

Christine Landfried, former professor of political science at Hamburg University, thinks the criticism that the court can be too political doesn't really make sense. Its purpose was always ultimately to make political decisions — but ones based on a legal argument, rather than a political debate.

"A constitutional court always deals with political questions," she told DW. "But the way that decisions are arrived at should follow legal arguments and legal methods. That's different from politics."

The court was founded in 1951, in the aftermath of World War II, to make sure that the laws of the newly founded West Germany adhered to the constitution, or Basic Law, which came into effect in 1949. Over the years, it has had to interpret the tenets of the Basic Law (democracy, human dignity, the rule of law) into many political questions: What happens to citizens' data? Should the government protect the climate? How much money should unemployed people be paid?
The importance of a plural court
Former Constitutional Court judge Gertrude Lübbe-Wolff thinks that the problem is not that the court is too political, but that its composition does not reflect new political realities in Germany.

As things stand, there is an agreement in the two houses of the German parliament, the Bundestag and the Bundesrat, that the main parties each propose a certain number of candidates for the court's two chambers, or senates. The Bundestag and the Bundesrat each pick half the judges for the two eight-seat senates.

That agreement was fractured, however, last year thanks to a campaign against an the candidate Frauke Brosius-Gersdorf, nominated by the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) whose position on decriminalizing abortion and other issues were deemed by some as too liberal. The campaign — driven by populist and unproven claims on social media — caused some parliamentarians from the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) to withdraw their support, before Brosius-Gersdorf herself withdrew her candidacy.

Though this affair may have damaged trust in how the court's judges were selected, Lübbe-Wolff argues that maintaining the court's plural composition is "extremely important for sensible and balanced decisions that are broadly accepted by the public," she told DW.
How a routine vote blew up German politics
German Constitutional Court vs the US Supreme Court

Unlike US Supreme Court judges, many of whom are familiar names whose opinions and party affiliation are widely known, the people who sit on Germany's Constitutional Court are not famous at all. But they are nominated by different parties in parliament, and their political affiliations are usually known to those who care to follow the nominations.

But a key difference to the US Supreme Court, Landfried points out, is that while in the US, the judges only have to agree on a decision, but each can write their own reasoning, the German Constitutional Court makes an effort to produce a joint reasoning for each decision, or a majority reasoning if some judges disagree. "The Federal Constitutional Court acts much more as an institution," she said. "It's considered very important that this or that senate made a decision, and not that individual judges are in the foreground."

Lübbe-Wolff's new book, entitled "Does the Federal Constitutional Court need (more) Reform?" contains a few ideas for how the court could be improved to make it less dependent on the choices of the political parties. One suggestion: Instead of having the different parties in the parliamentary committee propose candidates, the seats on the Constitutional Court would be advertised like any other job, and people would apply, and then have the committee decide on who to accept. This would, Lübbe-Wolff argues, maintain the democratic principles behind the court selection while reducing the influence of party politics. Austria and Switzerland both already have similar systems.
Landfried likes this idea. "That would mean party politics is not such a big part of the selection," she said. "Very good people could apply who haven't been chosen by the party."
Should there be AfD candidates for the court?

Lübbe-Wolff also believes that, for the sake of plurality, the Bundestag should allow candidates put forward by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) to be considered for the Constitutional Court. Germany's domestic intelligence agencies consider some sections of the AfD extremist and hostile to the constitution.

Indeed, the recent YouGov survey found that, among supporters of the major political parties, AfD supporters had by far the least faith in the court: Only 34%, compared to around 80% for both the CDU and SPD.
How much of a neo-Nazi party is the German AfD?
Nevertheless, some constitutional courts at the state level have already accepted AfD nominees into their ranks, notably Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg.

Now Lübbe-Wolff believes that the wider array of parties in the German parliament mean that the AfD and the socialist Left Party should also be allowed to propose candidates. "It used to be that the CDU and the SPD could simply decide between themselves which judges to elect," she said. "Today they always need votes from the Left Party too, because the AfD has become so big." She calls this imbalance a "structural problem."

But she believes that there are enough safeguards in the selection processes to ensure that no candidate for the Constitutional Court would hold views that were directly hostile to the constitution. "I think there are people who I believe are close enough to the AfD that the party could put them forward, but at the same time stand reliably on the foundation of the constitution," she said. "I think there are people of a younger generation in that category, but they don't want to out themselves."

Landfried is not sold on the idea. "For me, sections of that party is hostile to the constitution, it is partly right-wing extremist," she says, though she doesn't believe that all AfD voters are far-right. "But I have my reservations, and I wouldn't agree with that proposal."

Landfried is concerned that, because of Germany's Nazi history, the federal constitutional court should be especially wary about allowing people who potentially have far-right sympathies a place on the body that is, more than any other, meant to safeguard German democracy.
Edited by Rina Goldenberg

articles.title: What China's new military foothold in Laos means for Southeast Asia
articles.summary: Beijing says its new Laos facility will train pilots. Analysts see a broader signal: China's growing military presence in mainland Southeast Asia.

image.caption: The two communist nations said the Ban Keun center was aimed at training Lao air force pilotsImage: Vantor/REUTERS

blocks.text: China has opened a new military training and logistics facility in Laos, extending Beijing's security presence deeper into mainland Southeast Asia and potentially giving the Chinese air force its first dedicated foothold overseas.

The China-Laos Joint Support and Training Center at Ban Keun Airport, north of the capital Vientiane, formally began operations late last month alongside the new China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy.
Beijing says the center will primarily help train Lao air force pilots and will be jointly maintained and operated by the two countries.
The opening adds to China's still relatively small network of overseas military facilities.

Beijing established its first foreign military base in Djibouti in the Horn of Africa in 2017. A Chinese-funded expansion of Cambodia's Ream Naval Base was formally inaugurated last year, giving Chinese forces access to a facility strategically positioned near the South China Sea.
Laos and Cambodia are widely regarded as China's closest political partners in Southeast Asia, and military cooperation with both has expanded substantially in recent years.

"The two institutions … are not directed against any third party and aim to help further deepen practical cooperation between the two militaries and contribute to maintaining peace and stability in the region," said the Chinese Defense Ministry in a public statement.
Could Ban Keun become a permanent Chinese base?
The facility's infrastructure gives Beijing the option of expanding its military use in the future, Hunter Marston, director of the Southeast Asia Program at Australia's Lowy Institute, told DW.

"The focus may well be on joint training, but it has the potential to become a more permanent base. Should Beijing choose to use it as such, it has ample political leverage over Vientiane to demand exclusive access in the future," he added.
Laos has become heavily dependent on Chinese investment and financing during the past two decades. Critics have frequently accused Beijing of engaging in "debt-trap diplomacy."
The International Monetary Fund estimates Laos' public debt at around 81% of GDP last year, with China by far the largest bilateral creditor.

blocks.caption: China opened its first overseas military base in Djibouti in 2017, reflecting the Horn of Africa nation's strategic importanceImage: Xinhua/IMAGO

blocks.text: In 2020, China's state-owned China Southern Power Grid acquired a reported 90% stake in Electricite du Laos Transmission Company, which operates much of Laos' electricity transmission network.
A more durable Chinese military presence in Laos would also add another dimension to the strategic competition between Beijing and Washington in Southeast Asia.
The United States still enjoys far more extensive military access across the wider Indo-Pacific, particularly through alliances with the Philippines, Japan and Australia.

Beijing has historically lacked comparable overseas facilities. But Ban Keun, alongside Ream, could gradually reduce that disadvantage by giving the Chinese military additional locations from which to train, maintain equipment and potentially preposition supplies.
It is a particularly ominous development for Vietnam, Euan Graham, a senior fellow at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, told DW.
Hanoi and Beijing retain close party-to-party and economic relations, but they remain rivals in the South China Sea, where their competing territorial claims have repeatedly generated tensions.

Vietnam has also traditionally viewed Laos and Cambodia as strategically important buffers along its western flank and has worked for decades to maintain considerable political and military influence in both countries.

"Hanoi has always perceived the Indochinese peninsula as within its sphere of influence, offering a buffer against external aggressors, especially given Vietnam's narrow midriff," said Graham. "Now, it faces an alarming possibility of strategic encirclement by China. The new air base in Laos will certainly complicate Vietnam's defense planning."
Laos: A country in the grip of the Chinese?
Strategic importance should not be overstated
Other analysts caution, however, that geography places clear limits on Ban Keun's military value.

Collin Koh, a senior fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies at Singapore's Nanyang Technological University, told DW that China could gradually expand its presence at the facility.

Beijing could deploy more personnel, particularly advisers and instructors, as well as trainer aircraft and eventually more advanced aircraft, while also using the site to preposition equipment and supplies, he said.
But the "operational usefulness for the PLA's projection of military power in Southeast Asia is constrained by the landlocked nature of Laos."
Unlike Ream, Ban Keun provides no sea access, while Chinese military aircraft already operate from substantially larger and better-equipped bases in southern China.

While Vietnam will closely monitor Ban Keun for its potential role in any future South China Sea conflict, the site's geography doesn't give the Chinese military a significant operational advantage, said Koh.

Simon Creak, an associate professor at Singapore's National Institute of Education and a historian of Laos, noted that Vientiane has maintained a policy of non-alignment since adopting its current foreign policy in 1986.

"It has not had similar joint facilities in the past despite boasting close political and military relations with Vietnam, as well as China and Russia … and any mention of foreign bases in Laos typically recalls the CIA's bases during the Indochina Wars," Creak said.
Still, he believes it's "highly unlikely" that Laos will adjust its formal foreign policy settings or its longstanding effort to balance relations with Vietnam, Thailand and China.

articles.title: Germany news: Spy chief warns Russia conflict risk growing
articles.summary: Moscow is already waging a "shadow war" against Europe, the head of Germany's foreign intelligence service says. The Left Party is taking a case over remarks by the CDU's Katherina Reiche to a top…

image.caption: Martin Jäger, president of the BND, told a public hearing of the Bundestag's Parliamentary Oversight Committee that Russia was engaging in intimidtation attemptsImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: October 5, 2026
Chinese high-tech could be security risk — domestic intelligence agency
High-tech goods from China, such as electric vehicles or even robot vacuum cleaners, could represent a security risk, the BfV domestic intelligence agency has warned.
BfV head Sinan Selen told a hearing of parliament's intelligence oversight committee in Berlin that the issue was of "great concern" to him.
"I already see substantial shortcomings that create potential for abuse," he said.
Data collected via the products could be passed on to "state agencies", he said, leading to risks including "potential shutdown of entire products."
"In terms of resilience and availability (this) could confront us with problems," he said.
The warning comes as sales of high-tech products to Germany are growing and Chinese manufacturers compete ever more strongly with their German counterparts.

articles.title: Guardian readers fund life-changing surgery for Somali boy injured in US airstrike
articles.summary:
After Guardian investigation uncovered drone strike that killed 12 civilians and injured many more, seven-year-old Abdiqadir Salah underwent vital operation in Mogadishu

On the rickshaw ride…

blocks.text: On the rickshaw ride to the hospital, Marian Haji Abdi Guled felt a mixture of joy and apprehension: the day they had been waiting for had finally arrived.

Almost a year earlier, her then seven-year-old son, Abdiqadir Salah, had been seriously injured, alongside his two siblings, in what a Guardian investigation found was a US drone strike on the village of Jamaame in Somalia that killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children.
Abdiqadir’s small body had been impaled by shrapnel in the attack, and several chunks remained embedded in his back.

Doctors feared that without an operation to remove them, the boy would lose his ability to walk, but Guled had no money for an operation. For 10 months, the family had languished in Mogadishu with growing expenses and no income – unable to afford surgery, but unwilling to let the boy return to the village without it.
After the investigation, which told the story of Guled and other civilians affected by the attack, a group of Guardian readers from across the globe fundraised for Abdiqadir’s surgery and recovery.
Within a few hours, enough money was raised to cover his treatment and rehabilitation, as well as any medical expenses and treatment for her other two children, who sustained less extensive injuries.
“I was so happy when I found out that Guardian readers raised the money needed for my son’s surgery. I didn’t know people like this existed,” Guled said.
“The people who contributed to the surgery – I really appreciate their support and how they stood by our family when we needed it the most.”
On a Saturday morning in September, Guled waited anxiously as Abdiqadir was finally taken for surgery at Kaafi hospital in Mogadishu.

“Other patients were taken into surgery after him and came out before him – so I worried maybe something went wrong,” she said. “I got to a point where I knocked on the operating room door asking if my son was still alive, then was held back by other patients.”

Finally, her son emerged. Doctors told Guled the surgery had been successful, but complex. While the first two pieces of shrapnel from the missile had been successfully removed, taking out the final piece was considered too risky, possibly resulting in paralysis, so they concluded that it was safer to leave it and monitor his condition.

When the Guardian visited Abdiqadir a few weeks later, he appeared bright, energised and visibly happy. “I have one piece of metal still in me, and if they touch it, I might become paralysed,” the seven-year-old said. “[But] I don’t have any problem with the last piece of metal in my body, because I’m no longer in pain.”

The Guardian investigation into the US airstrikes that injured Abduqadir raised myriad questions about US military intelligence, such as how the targets were selected and why children were hit while they were clearly visible and out in the open. The US has not responded to any questions about the Jamaame attack.

In the months since then, US attacks on the area have continued: from December 2025 to July 2026, it carried out at least three airstrikes around Jamaame, according to research by New America, a security thinktank that documents US military operations abroad. Residents say drones continue to fly above the town.

“We cannot return to Jamaame because what caused my children to be hurt is still there,” Guled said. “I fled Jamaame with my wounded children because of the drones, and the drones are still [flying].”

With the remaining financial support she received from Guardian readers, Guled plans to relocate with her children to the government-controlled port city of Kismayo, which has not been the target of drone strikes, and where Abdiqadir can receive further surgery if needed.
She still wants answers from the US government, nearly a year after they were bombed. “My son has been left scarred for life,” she said.
“I want the US government be held accountable for what they did to my family and for the US to stop bombing our community.”

articles.title: Suspected pneumonic plague in Siberia: What we know about the disease
articles.summary: A worker at a plague research institute in Siberia has died, and nearly 200 of her contacts are under medical observation. Russian authorities deny a link to the bacterial infection. The US is…

image.caption: Image: Britta Pedersen/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What you need to know about plague

items: There are three forms of plague, all caused by the bacterium, Yersinia pestis.
The three forms of plague are bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.

Bubonic plague is the most common form; it does not spread from person-to-person. If untreated, the bacteria can move through the body and bloodstream, causing septicemic plague, which causes internal bleeding and organ failure, and if they reach the lungs, they cause pneumonic plague.
Pneumonic plague is highly contagious as it can pass from person to person through the air, via coughing, for example.
If untreated, bubonic plague kills between 30-60% of patients. The septicemic and pneumonic forms are always fatal without treatment.

blocks.text: Speculation over the death in a Russian plague laboratory

Following the death of a Russian laboratory worker, there is speculation about an outbreak of pneumonic plague, a highly contagious bacterial infection of the lungs. Russia denies there is a broader risk to the community.

Russian officials have said the laboratory worker's death was not caused by a plague pathogen. The 28-year-old died of "pneumonia of unknown origin," according to Russia's Interfax news agency, citing Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's disease-control agency. According to that agency, samples taken from the woman showed no microorganisms "related to her professional activities." This contradicts earlier information.
Local media had previously reported that the woman, who worked at an institute dedicated to fighting plague, had dropped a test tube.
She reportedly died on Friday, October 2, 2026, at the district hospital in Shelekhov, a town near Irkutsk in Siberia.

According to official Russian figures, two hospitals and a children's clinic were placed under quarantine. Local reports said staff at the institute were being quarantined at their workplace. The US news site Axios has reported that around 200 people who had been in contact with the woman had been placed under observation. There were no further reported infections.

Even so, distrust of how Russia handles information persists. On one of DW's Russian-language social media channels, a user wrote: "It wouldn't surprise me if this turns into a disaster now, both in terms of the spread and the quarantine measures."
Pneumonic plague: a fast-moving lung infection
All that is known for certain, at time of writing and first publication (October 5, 2026), is that pneumonic plague is highly contagious.

Pneumonic plague is a form of plague that infects the lungs. Like every form of the disease, it is caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium usually found in small mammals, such as rodents and in the fleas that feed on them.
The World Health Organization describes the pneumonic form as the most virulent type of plague.

Its incubation period can be as short as 24 hours, and it is the only form that passes easily from person to person through respiratory particles released when a sick patient coughs. This is why, according to the WHO, it can trigger severe epidemics.
Symptoms appear quickly: high fever, headache and weakness, followed by a rapidly worsening pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain and a cough that often brings up blood.
A person can catch pneumonic plague by breathing in the bacteria directly, or by developing it when bubonic and/or septicemic go untreated and spread to the lungs.
What is the difference between bubonic and pneumonic plague
Pneumonic plague is not a separate disease. It is one of three forms of plague: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.
All are caused by the same bacterium.
What sets them apart is where the infection settles in the body, and that shapes how the disease spreads and how deadly it is.

Bubonic plague is the most common form and the one most people think of when they hear "plague". It usually follows a flea bite. The bacteria travel to the nearest lymph node, which swells into a painful lump known as a bubo. According to the WHO, it rarely spreads between people.

If bubonic plague goes untreated, the bacteria can move further through the body. If they spread into the bloodstream, the disease can become septicemic plague, which causes bleeding under the skin, tissue death in the fingers and toes, and organ failure. If the bacteria reach the lungs, the illness becomes pneumonic plague, the form that can pass from person to person through the air. Both septicemic and pneumonic plague can also develop directly, without a bubo appearing first.
Left untreated, bubonic plague kills between 30-60% of patients. The septicaemic and pneumonic forms are always fatal without treatment.
Pneumonic plague treatment: antibiotics within the first 24 hours
Pneumonic plague is curable, but only if treatment starts quickly. The WHO warns that without treatment it can kill within 18 to 24 hours of the first symptoms.
Common antibiotics can cure the infection, and recovery rates are high when patients are treated within about a day of falling ill.

Speed is what decides the outcome. Doctors are advised not to wait for laboratory confirmation and to start antibiotics as soon as plague is suspected, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The drugs themselves are not rare or specialized. They are standard, widely used antibiotics, and patients usually need a course of up to two weeks. To stop the infection spreading, patients are kept in isolation, and wearing masks helps protect those around them, the WHO says.
Preventive antibiotics and isolation for close contacts

People who were close to a patient are treated as well, even if they have no symptoms. Both the WHO and the CDC recommend a seven-day course of preventive antibiotics for close contacts of anyone with pneumonic plague.
The WHO does not recommend a plague vaccine for the public. It reserves vaccination for high-risk groups, such as laboratory staff who work with the bacterium and health workers.

articles.title: German soccer: Can new coach Klopp turn things around?
articles.summary: Jürgen Klopp has done things a little differently since becoming Germany coach. Casting a wider net for talent and trying to connect with players and country haven't made an immediate impact, but he…

image.caption: Jürgen Klopp handed debuts to a number of young players in his first internationals Image: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Four games, three goals, two draws, one loss and one win. Jürgen Klopp would have hoped for better results from his first international break as Germany coach. But though the comfortable win over Serbia (2-0), draws against the Netherlands (1-1) and Greece (0-0) and a shock loss to Greece (0-1) in Germany leave them third out of four in their Nations League group, Klopp saw mostly positives.

"Everyone showed what they're made of; everyone earned their place. We've shown signs that we can do some things better than people gave us credit for. I wanted to get something going, and I definitely saw that happen," he said after Sunday's 0-0 draw in Thessaloniki.
For all the positivity of the former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach, the four matches have, in reality, been a mixed bag for Germany.
It's a long road back to the top
Having fallen in the last 32 of the 2026 World Cup and exited in the group stage in 2022, Germany's footballing stock has never been lower.

Klopp tried to address this by casting his net wider, announcing a 44-man squad that split over the matches. He then said this would be a one off, but that his strategy of trying to find a diamond in the relative rough who could adapt to the international game had given him valuable insights.

blocks.caption: Germany have exited early at the last two World CupsImage: Uwe Kraft/IMAGO

blocks.text: "Hard work, lots of information — these guys are brimming with talent," he said of those given a surprise opportunity.
"People were saying that German soccer was at rock bottom and that there was no talent. ... They're not lacking in talent."
While Klopp may have seen potential, and has credit in the bank from his past work, he will need to turn that into results before too long.
Klopp leans on emotion and unity

While much has been said about Klopp's success in imprinting his trademark Gegenpressing (counter press) style early on, he is also a coach who places a high value on connection. Throughout the international break, he has worn a cap emblazoned with the slogan "Einer von 83 millionen” (One of 83 million) in a reference to the German population and an attempt to unify in a country divided by the rise of the far-right AfD party.
He addressed the issue in his opening press conference and then reiterated his position after some social media users branded the team "not white enough" after their loss to Greece.

"There is no reason to give these people any thought. They aren't getting any of my attention. I have little time for stupidity in real life and none on social media either," Klopp said in answer to a question posed by DW.
As well as speaking honestly about his country, Klopp has been open with his new players.

"He has a very good rapport with every player. He tries to reach out to every player and make them feel good, that they're important and that they deserve to be here," said Florian Wirtz, who went on to label his coach as a "master" at managing relationships.
With limited time together, forming bonds between player, coach and country can elevate a national team. It may prove to be more important than any tactical plans.
Havertz injury highlights lack of striking depth

One of the key men in the more senior squad that started the opener against the Netherlands, Kai Havertz limped off after 29 minutes. He was replaced by Eintracht Frankfurt's Younes Ebnoutalib while Nick Woltemade (on loan at Juventus from Newcastle) and Jonathan Burkhardt, also Frankfurt, were also tested up front over the four games.

None of the replacements scored, with Woltemade guilty of a particularly bad miss against Serbia and Burkhardt having a goal disallowed against Greece on Sunday. While all have potential and have enjoyed strong patches of form in their careers, none is tried and tested at the top level, and none is playing in the Champions League. With Havertz being somewhat injury prone, Klopp needs someone to emerge as a viable backup.
Musiala and Wirtz key but both have question marks

Injury is also, sadly, beginning to be a major feature of Jamal Musiala's career. He picked up a thigh injury in the warmup to the Netherlands game that may keep him out for a month. He's also missed games this season due to a neurological condition and missed the first half of last season with a broken leg which came soon after another lengthy spell out. At his best, he is probably Germany's brightest attacking spark, but it's been a while since that level has been seen.

blocks.caption: There are signs that Florian Wirtz could thrive in Jürgen Klopp's systemImage: Tom Weller/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: For Wirtz, the issue is slightly different. He was excellent in the win over a limited Serbia team, scoring one and creating the other. It was a reminder of a talent that has been largely dormant at Liverpool where he's shown his creative best only in glimpses. He followed it up with a decent display against Greece but saw Burkahrdt inadvertently block his goalbound header. There were signs Klopp's system may suit him.
"He's really gotten us on board with his philosophy," said Wirtz of his coach. "I enjoy it myself, too. I get to show my strengths when we have possession."
Klopp will need more of the same from Wirtz, who captained the side in Greece, if Germany are to move forward.

articles.title: Bosnia election: New steps to prevent electoral fraud, but nationalist parties remain on top
articles.summary: New technology has stopped votes being cast on behalf of dead or absent voters, and turnout has fallen to a record low. But it was a case of deja vu in Bosnia's elections with the same parties…

image.caption: Voter turnout in the Bosnian elections reached a record low of just over 40% on SundayImage: AFP

blocks.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina went to the polls on October 4 with new technology that was meant to end years of vote-rigging.
Chief among the abuses was the casting of ballots in the name of deceased voters who had lingered for years on outdated voter rolls.
At just over 40%, turnout was the lowest since the Bosnian War ended in 1995, in part because the old tricks no longer worked.

In earlier elections, allegations kept surfacing that votes were being cast in the name of people who had died or long since moved abroad. Others said voters cast their ballot multiple times or that blank ballots were added after polls closed to make the turnout look higher.

blocks.caption: New technology was introduced in these elections in an attempt to stop vote-riggingImage: Dragan Maksimović/DW

blocks.text: The voter registry, packed with names of people who had passed away or left the country, was the perfect tool for all of this.
New technology, same old politics
This time, however, every polling station used biometric fingerprint checks.
This represented a clear step forward in making voter identification far harder to manipulate.
Still, the biggest story of this election is not technical. Three nationalist parties won, each within its own community: the SNSD among Serbs, the SDA among Bosniaks and the HDZ BiH among Croats.
The dead may have been struck from the voter rolls, but political trends have not shifted.

For readers who know Bosnia only vaguely, a little background helps: The 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement ended the war, but it also split the country into two entities: Republika Srpska, which has a Serb majority, and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which has a Bosniak-Croat majority.
A three-member presidency runs the state, and each of the three peoples elects its own member.
That is why elections here are rarely about wages and prices and are instead almost always about who is perceived to be a threat.
Republika Srpska and the return of a fallen leader
For Milorad Dodik, the most powerful Serb politician in Bosnia, this election was a political resurrection.
In 2025, Dodik was barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the high representative, the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process.
He was sanctioned by the US in 2022, although those sanctions were lifted late last year. Even so, his party, the SNSD, virtually swept the board in Republika Srpska.
Savo Minic became president of Republika Srpska, and Zeljka Cvijanovic kept the Serb seat in the presidency. Both are members of the SNSD.

The party also did very well in the entity's parliament. Neither the sanctions nor Dodik's conviction and the loss of his mandate hurt the party. Voters were not choosing an individual. They were choosing their "side."

blocks.caption: Milorad Dodik, the former President of Republika Srpska, says his party has retained power in the majority-Serb entity and its seat on the shared presidency at national levelImage: AFP

blocks.text: Dodik lost no time in declaring what comes next.

He announced a return to what he refers to as the "original Dayton." In practice, that means undoing the powers the state has gained since 1995 — from the judiciary to the army. To an outside observer, that sounds like a technical phrase. In reality, it is a program for dismantling the state step by step.
"That means we are returning the army to Republika Srpska, the border police, the intelligence service and everything that the high representatives once took away," said Dodik.
A deal between Serbs and Croats?
The opposition offered no serious resistance. It was divided and had no convincing message.
Voters who did not want Dodik had nowhere to turn, so most stayed home. Low turnout favored the side with the most disciplined party machine.

That raises a question that will shape what happens in Bosnia in the coming year. Dodik's conviction kept him out of the direct race in these elections. But for months, there has been talk of a way out.

If representatives of the SNSD and the HDZ BiH enter the presidency, they could pardon him — whatever the third member decides. Bosnian media have reported that this was a pre-election deal between Dodik and the HDZ BiH leader, Dragan Covic. Dodik could then return as prime minister of Republika Srpska, a post he has held before.
Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina: Troika defeated
The picture in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina is different, but the outcome is the same.

blocks.caption: 'The future of our region lies not in adopting the Russian model but the European one. The message to the EU: Help Bosnia,' said Denis Becirovic of the Social Democrats after the preliminary results were announcedImage: Amel Emric/REUTERS

blocks.text: The parties of the so-called "Troika," a multi-ethnic liberal political alliance, suffered a defeat. They came to power at this level after the international high representative, a foreigner with the authority to impose laws, changed the election law.
Voters saw no benefit from that experiment. The SDA, the largest Bosniak nationalist party, won the most seats and did well.

The paradox is that SDA president Bakir Izetbegovic lost the race for the presidency. He is the son of Alija Izetbegovic, Bosnia's first president and one of the signatories of the Dayton agreement. The winner was Denis Becirovic of the Social Democrats (SDP), who kept the Bosniak seat.
So, the party won the election, but its leader lost. The son of the man who signed Dayton is now shut out of the institution Dayton created.

"The future of our region lies not in adopting the Russian model but the European one. The message to the EU: Help Bosnia. Let the will of the people be the law of the land," Becirovic said as he declared victory.
A Croat surprise

The same pattern holds among Croats. Darijana Filipovic of the HDZ BiH, their strongest nationalist party, won the Croat seat in the presidency for her party. Filipovic spent years as an aide to Covic, the Bosnian Croat leader.
"HDZ BiH has shown it is brave enough to take a road others would not dare. Who would have dared to nominate me? To some too young, but a surprise to everyone," Filipovic said after the vote.

blocks.caption: Darijana Filipovic, a candidate of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina (HDZ BiH) won the Croat seat of the presidency on SundayImage: Amel Emric/REUTERS

blocks.text: Three peoples, three nationalist parties, three victories, and not one conversation about how to keep people in the country.
What this means for the state

The most important thing about these elections is not the numbers but the makeup of the presidency. Two women will sit in it: Cvijanovic of the SNSD and Filipovic of the HDZ BiH. Anyone who tries to sell that as a breakthrough for women in politics has missed the point.
Both come from parties that, in different ways, do not want the state in its current form. Both could also decide the fate of a man convicted of defying the international oversight of Dayton.

The HDZ BiH has long demanded a third, Croat entity. The SNSD wants autonomy for Republika Srpska. One side wants to split the state into three, the other into two, but they share the aim of making it smaller.
So, the presidency, which should symbolize a shared state, is again made up of people who feel like guests in it.

All of this is happening as the Western Balkans again becomes a stage for rivalry between Russia, the EU and the US. Dodik openly thanked both Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump after his party's victory.

Bosnia has entered a new electoral era with new technology and old politics. Young people are leaving the country in droves. The dead no longer vote, but the living have stopped believing that anything can be different.

articles.title: Trump heads to Nebraska in attempt to shore up GOP’s midterm vote – US politics live
articles.summary: President to visit Grand Island as his plan to allow more foreign beef imports proves unpopular in agriculture-rich state

blocks.text: Key events

items: 24m agoTrump heads to Nebraska in attempt to shore up the GOP's midterm vote

blocks.caption: Robert Mackey

blocks.text: Robert Mackey
The White House has defended a newly hired press aide who posed for a holiday photograph in 2021 wearing a “Fuck Joe Biden” T-shirt and holding a rifle.

Beni Rae Harmony, the new assistant White House press secretary, revealed on Friday that she was going to work for Donald Trump just days after covering him as a correspondent for Real America’s Voice, a partisan rightwing outlet originally created as a video podcast platform for the president’s former adviser Steve Bannon.

According to a LinkedIn profile, Harmony, 24, previously worked as a producer for the far-right Turning Point USA host Jack Posobiec – and as a press aide “focusing on crisis management” for two far-right Republicans: congressman Paul Gosar of Arizona and former congressman Matt Gaetz of Florida.

In 2021, when Gosar was censured by the US House for posting an animated video that depicted him killing Democratic congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and attacking Joe Biden, Harmony recorded an outraged defense of her boss for his YouTube channel.

The photograph of Harmony and an older man posing with rifles in matching anti-Biden shirts, in front of Christmas decorations, was reportedly posted on Instagram in November 2021 by a far-right Republican House candidate, Jarome Bell, who mounted a failed campaign for Congress in 2022.
Trump heads to Nebraska in attempt to shore up the GOP's midterm vote
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Donald Trump will be in Nebraska later today, campaigning alongside Republican senator Pete Ricketts, in an attempt to salvage the GOP’s dwindling midterms campaign.

The president is headed to Grand Island, located in the solidly conservative south-central part of the state. It’s part of what Trump says is a 32-day blitz of rallies ahead of 3 November that so far has taken him to ruby-red territory such as Oklahoma and Alabama.
On Wednesday, he will make his second stop in two weeks in Texas with a rally in San Antonio.

“The president’s coming to Nebraska to help me campaign, so I can get reelected,” Ricketts, who is running against an independent candidate backed by national Democrats, told the Associated Press last week on Capitol Hill.

The administration’s plan to allow more imports of foreign beef has particularly roiled the agriculture-rich state of Nebraska. Trump wants to lower beef prices for consumers but ranchers have rebelled against the import proposal, arguing it would undercut them.

“The plan to import low-quality foreign beef is not helping Nebraska ranchers,” Ricketts told the AP. “I would advise the White House to change that policy and look for longer-term things that will help us build the size of the herd and ultimately bring the price of beef down for consumers.”

This campaign is set against the president’s plummeting approval ratings, the unravelling of his Maga movement and an affordability crisis escalated by his unpopular war on Iran. But Trump supporters are also among the most motivated to vote and Republicans have far deeper coffers to mobilise their base.
Meanwhile, vice-president JD Vance will rally in Alaska for senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican locked in a tight reelection campaign.
In other developments:

items: The White House has defended a newly hired press aide who posed for a holiday photograph in 2021 wearing a “Fuck Joe Biden” T-shirt and holding a rifle. Beni Rae Harmony, the new assistant White House press secretary, revealed on Friday that she was going to work for Donald Trump just days after covering him as a correspondent for Real America’s Voice, a partisan rightwing outlet originally created as a video podcast platform for the president’s former adviser Steve Bannon.

Trump on Sunday named Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, to also serve as the new White House AI czar. Clayton, who leads the US’s 18 intelligence agencies, previously served as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and led the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term.

The United States has removed ⁠its B-1 bombers from a ⁠British air base one ​week after five men were arrested nearby on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts, a suspected plot that British prime minister Andy Burnham said was likely backed by Iran. The planes had been stationed at ⁠RAF Fairford, the preferred European base for US bombers 90 miles west of London, which had recently been used for US strikes on Iran.

articles.title: Southern Manitoba First Nations condemn newspaper for column questioning deaths at residential schools
articles.summary: A column questioning the deaths of children at residential schools has led the Southern Chiefs’ Organization to condemn the Winnipeg Sun and express concern that the newspaper’s CEO is running for…

image.caption: People march through downtown Winnipeg on the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on Sept. 30. (Prabhjot Singh Lotey/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba

A column questioning the deaths of children at residential schools has led the Southern Chiefs’ Organization to condemn the Winnipeg Sun and express concern that the newspaper’s CEO is running for mayor of the Manitoba capital.
Column published days after National Day for Truth and Reconciliation; Kevin Klein disavows responsibility

A column questioning the deaths of children at residential schools has led the Southern Chiefs' Organization to condemn the Winnipeg Sun and express concern that the newspaper's CEO is running for mayor of the Manitoba capital.

On Oct. 4, the Sun published a column entitled "Grave misdirection: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence," suggesting the deaths of Indigenous children at residential schools have been mischaracterized.
"Each death is a tragedy, but none is evidence of an atrocity," the column states, citing as examples the death of one child from bronchitis and another by lightning.

The National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation documented the deaths of at least 4,200 Indigenous children over the course of 165 years at Canada's residential schools. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada defined the deaths and widespread abuses within residential schools as cultural genocide.

The publication of the column four days after the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation led to a formal statement of condemnation from the Southern Chiefs' Organization, which represents 33 Anishinaabe and Dakota First Nations in Manitoba.

"Survivors and their families should not be forced, yet again, to prove what happened to them or defend the children who never came home," SCO Grand Chief Jerry Daniels said in a statement. "Thousands of children died while attending residential schools. Children were forcibly removed from their families and Nations, stripped of their languages and cultures, and subjected to systems of abuse, neglect and assimilation.
"These are not allegations or political talking points. They are part of Canada's documented historical record."

The co-author of a book about residential school denialism called the column disgusting because, he said, it perpetuates the notion the deaths of thousands of children who were forcibly removed from their families is less horrific because many died of disease, malnutrition and neglect as opposed to murder.

"A lot of people will say, oh, it was just tuberculosis. Lots of kids died of tuberculosis in the early 20th century," said University of Manitoba history professor Sean Carleton, the co-author of Truth Before Reconciliation: Confronting Residential School Denialism.

"That, in fact, is true, except for the fact that, you know what spreads tuberculosis faster? Overcrowding, poor nutrition. Lack of proper sanitation, overwork. All of these issues that were known to be systemic to the residential school system."
Carleton said the column perpetuates what he describes as far-right misinformation about First Nations making claims about mass graves or clandestine murders.

"This is a distraction tactic. It's an attempt to move the goalposts, to make it extremely difficult for Indigenous nations, to explain the complicated nuanced understanding of what we already know, thanks to church and state records, that at least 4,000 children died in these institutions for a variety of different reasons," he said.

items: Why these Sask. writers contributed to a new book about residential school denialism

blocks.text: As criticism of the column mounted Sunday, the editor-in-chief of the Klein Group, the company that owns the Winnipeg Sun, dug in her heels. Heather Klein defended the column in a followup entitled "Disagreement is not denial."
The Southern Chiefs' Organization also criticized her husband, Klein Group CEO Kevin Klein, the candidate who is running for Winnipeg mayor.

Daniels called it "deeply concerning" someone seeking public office provided a platform for someone to use residential schools and the deaths of First Nations children as the basis for political commentary.

"Winnipeg is home to a large and vibrant First Nations population. Anyone asking to lead this city has a responsibility to understand the history of residential schools and the ongoing responsibilities of reconciliation," Daniels said.
Kevin Klein said in a statement he is not responsible for the content of the Winnipeg Sun while he runs for mayor.

"From the day I entered the race for mayor, I stepped away from every editorial decision at the Winnipeg Sun, and I have kept that commitment. The paper stands on its own," the mayoral candidate said.
Heather Klein alone is responsible for the content, he said, adding he does not assign stories, edit copy, approve pieces, or stop them from running.
"Any suggestion otherwise is reckless and without foundation," he said.
Other mayoral candidates criticize Klein
Several mayoral candidates also criticized the newspaper CEO-turned-candidate.
Mayoral candidate Noah Redden said in a statement there is a difference between upholding freedom of speech and tolerating hate speech.
Redden called residential-school denialism inflammatory and said Klein needs to explain to Winnipeg's Indigenous population why his newspaper echoed attacks on residential-school survivors.
Mayoral candidate Scott Gillingham told reporters Sunday he's spoken to enough Indigenous families in Winnipeg to hear firsthand the impact of residential schools.

"What is not deniable in my mind is the impact, the lasting, devastating impact of residential schools on our country," said Gillingham, who attended TRC Day events in an official capacity on Wednesday.
Klein said Friday he did not attend TRC Day events but called the national holiday important.
"Canadians ought to know what took place in the residential school system and what it has meant for Indigenous families and communities ever since," Klein said Sunday in a statement.
"The wrongs of the past should not be forgotten. As a father and a grandfather, I cannot begin to imagine the pain those families carry."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Bartley Kives joined CBC Manitoba in 2016. Prior to that, he spent three years at the Winnipeg Sun and then 18 at the Winnipeg Free Press, writing about politics, music, food and outdoor recreation. He's the author of three books — two of them Canadian bestsellers — and the winner of a Canadian Screen Award for reporting.

articles.title: Quebec poised to elect separatists to power for first time more than decade
articles.summary:
Parti Québécois promises to hold independence referendum in Canada’s French-speaking region by 2028

Voters in Quebec are going to the polls in provincial elections which will probably result…

blocks.text: Voters in Quebec are going to the polls in provincial elections which will probably result in victory for a party that has promised to hold a referendum on independence from Canada within the next two years.

If polls are correct, the Parti Québécois (PQ) will form the government of the province of roughly nine million, the first time that the separatist movement will have gained power in the French-speaking region for more than a decade.
A PQ victory in Monday’s election would also be likely to trigger a return to pitched battles over questions of language and identity between Quebec and the federal government.

Long considered a declining force in Quebec politics, the PQ owes its resurgence to party leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon. The 49-year-old Oxford-educated lawyer and polyglot has positioned himself as a TikToking gen-X rebuttal to François Legault, Quebec’s long-serving Premier until he resigned early this year.

blocks.caption: Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is greeted by his children and partner ahead of a leaders debate in Montreal in September. Photograph: Canadian Press/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Analysts say that St-Pierre Plamondon’s electoral success is not because he is a separatist – the majority of voters do not support an independent Quebec – but because of his rightwing take on red-meat identity issues.

He has blamed immigrants for Quebec’s overflowing schools, increased crime and skyrocketing housing prices, while promising to slash immigration levels and ban “conspicuous” religious symbols from the bodies of teachers and their students. He has derided his critics from the leftist Quebec Solidaire party as “woke”, and has taken to repeating the talking points of hard-right columnists.

Many in the province agree with St-Pierre Plamondon’s rhetoric, even though it strays from PQ’s social democratic roots, according to radio host Patrick Lagacé. “Most Quebecers traditionally see themselves as being on the left. Increasingly, though, they are on the right when it comes to social issues like systemic racism and accommodation of religious behaviour. They’ve hardened on these issues, and don’t see themselves in the left’s recent fixation on identity issues,” Lagacé said.

The biggest drag on St-Pierre Plamondon’s popularity has been his oft-repeated promise to hold a referendum during the first mandate of a PQ government. An overwhelming majority of Quebecers don’t want such a thing any time soon – particularly with Canada locked in a trade war with the US. The province mostly voted for Liberal leader Mark Carney over the separatist Bloc Québécois in last year’s federal election, expressly because of Carney’s “elbows up” posturing against the Trump administration.

But for the PQ, Donald Trump was at first a curse, then a gift. Early in the campaign, St-Pierre Plamondon said he wouldn’t hold a referendum as long as Trump was in power, defusing the issue and allowing St-Pierre Plamondon to concentrate on attacking immigration and immigrants.

The party has also benefited from a four-way race for the right-leaning nationalist vote beyond the reliably Liberal fiefdom of Montreal – particularly around Quebec city, where the upstart Parti Conservateur du Québec has made significant inroads. “The Parti Québécois is benefiting from a massive vote split because those who don’t like the PQ don’t agree on who to vote for,” said poll analyst Philippe Fournier.

Though the PQ will probably form the next provincial government, it remains unclear what sort of mandate it will have. Polls have the party hovering at roughly 30%, somewhat below the likely threshold for a majority government.

In any case, St-Pierre Plamondon is laying the groundwork for confrontation with the federal government. He has mused about defunding the office of Quebec’s lieutenant-governor (the British Crown’s representative in the province) and promised to introduce a law to abolish the province’s ties with the monarchy, which separatists see as the ultimate symbol of oppression of Canada’s French minority.

St-Pierre Plamondon also tore into Carney, after the prime minister said the government will probably increase immigration rates in the country. Doing so, St-Pierre Plamondon said, was an “abuse of power” that would have further nefarious effects on French-language services in Quebec.
For a man who trades on his relative youthfulness, St-Pierre Plamondon’s attacks on the monarchy have the whiff of anachronism – the kind of thing the PQ did in its 1970-era heyday.

Attacking the federal government is similarly outdated, and potentially risky for St-Pierre Plamondon. Carney remains popular in Quebec, and is likely to remain so, at least until the existential threat of Trump recedes.

articles.title: Sass Jordan, Canadian rock singer-songwriter, dies aged 65
articles.summary:
Musician who had hit albums with Racine and Rats later became a judge on six seasons of Canadian Idol

Sass Jordan, the singer-songwriter who became a significant success in Canada’s rock…

blocks.text: Sass Jordan, the singer-songwriter who became a significant success in Canada’s rock scene in the 1990s before starring as a judge on Canadian Idol, has died aged 65.

No cause of death has been given. A statement on social media said she died on 2 October “surrounded by her loving family … She remains in our hearts, an inimitable force of nature. An irreplaceable being of light and joy!”

Born in Birmingham, England, in 1960, Jordan moved to Montreal as a child when her French academic father took a position at the city’s Concordia University. She began performing in her teens, and by her 20s was recording with a range of Montreal acts: she wrote a song for singer Michael Breen that became a Canadian Top 40 hit.

By 1988 she was signed to Atlantic Records, who released her debut album Tell Somebody, with two singles – the title track and Double Trouble – charting just outside the Canadian Top 10. The following year she won a Juno (the Canadian equivalent of the Grammys) for most promising female vocalist.

Her 1992 album Racine contained four Canadian Top 20 hits and, coupled with a move to Los Angeles, a new label in RCA, and an appearance on the bestselling soundtrack to The Bodyguard broke Jordan into a wider US market. Sun’s Gonna Rise, from 1994 album Rats, became her only US Hot 100 hit, and her biggest hit in Canada, reaching No 7. Taylor Hawkins, later the drummer for Foo Fighters, was her live drummer during this period.

Her RCA deal ended and Jordan later voiced disappointment in the glossy sound of her next couple of albums, but her career received a boost from being a judge on the six seasons of TV talent show Canadian Idol, and she returned to recording with 2006’s You Get What You Give. In 2001 she also performed as Janis Joplin in the off-Broadway musical Love, Janis.
She later embraced a bluesier sound, with 2020 album Rebel Moon Blues reaching the top five of the US blues chart, followed by her most recent studio recording, 2022’s Bitches Blues.
In September, Jordan cancelled tour dates, citing “a serious medical condition”.

articles.title: How Spain's housing crisis has resulted in an early general election
articles.summary: his series of measures to tackle the housing crisis was defeated in parliament on Friday

blocks.text: Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez confirmed Spain will be heading to the polls on 29 November, after Sanchez's Socialist party, which is currently heading a minority government, failed to pass housing reforms in the Spanish Congress.

Sanchez faces an uphill battle in his bid for re-election with polls showing Sánchez's Socialist party is trailing the conservative People's Party - which many expect to attempt to form a government with the far-right Vox.

In his statement announcing the election, Sanchez warned Spaniards about what he called the "extreme-right wave" being seen in other countries and said Spain should continue to be a global example of "peace, feminism and prosperity".
BBC correspondent Guy Hedgecoe reports.
Follow the BBC's live coverage following Sanchez's announcement.

articles.title: Extreme heat warnings issued for parts of southern California
articles.summary:
Temperatures in US state forecast to hit high 30s celsius this week, while regions in Indonesia grapple with wildfires

The National Weather Service in the US has issued extreme heat warnings…

blocks.text: The National Weather Service in the US has issued extreme heat warnings for parts of southern California, including Los Angeles, until Thursday, as temperatures are expected to hit the high 30s celsius. Burbank, a suburb north of Los Angeles, recorded 39C on Saturday, a few degrees shy of the October record for the region set in 1987. A persistent area of high pressure will remain in place this week, leading to further hazardous hot weather and increased fire risk.

Parts of Indonesia are in the midst of an extreme wildfire season, which has peaked over the past month. Western Kalimantan (Borneo) and southern Sumatra have been particularly badly affected. The lack of rainfall has dried the usually water-logged tropical soils, meaning that fires have been able to spread quickly, above and below the surface. Indonesia’s soils are also extremely rich in peat, meaning that the smoke produced from the fires contain higher levels of toxic gases such as sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide. Cities in surrounding areas and as far as Malaysia and Singapore have experienced reduced air quality in recent weeks as a result. Drought and wildfires are more common in this part of the world during El Niño events owing to suppressed thunderstorm activity.

blocks.caption: Indonesian firefighters work to extinguish wildfires near a residential area in Palembang, south Sumatra. Photograph: Muhammad Fajri/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: On the flip side, El Niño is contributing to an extremely active period for tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean. After recent hurricanes in the eastern half of the basin, Super Typhoon Choi-Wan is now active and a category 4 typhoon to the south-east of Japan, while on a strengthening trend. After developing on 30 September, Choi-Wan moved through the Northern Mariana Islands as a tropical storm, causing power outages on the island of Tinian, forcing the closure of schools and government offices. Choi-Wan underwent rapid intensification after clearing the islands on Sunday, and as of Sunday night has sustained winds of 150mph, and gusts of up to 180mph. The system is expected to curve away from mainland Japan and areas affected by Typhoon Dujuan last month, while steadily weakening over the coming week.

articles.title: Spain’s Sánchez to hold press conference amid speculation over early election – Europe live
articles.summary:
PM may call a vote to address national housing crisis after parliament rejected two of his government’s emergency relief measures

Good morning and welcome to our Europe live blog.

…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 8m agoMorning opening: Spain's Sánchez to speak amid speculation over early election

blocks.text: Morning opening: Spain's Sánchez to speak amid speculation over early election

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa

Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez is about to hold a press conference shortly amid speculation he is about to call a snap election to address a national housing crisis, after parliament rejected two of his government’s emergency relief measures on Friday.
The vote prompted tens of thousands to march in the street on Saturday, in the capital Madrid and other cities. Protesters were calling for action on rent prices and tenant protections.
Spain’s next general election had been due next year, and Sánchez had previously said that he would complete a full four-year term.

But the defeats in parliament have raised questions on how effective his government can be in getting through key legislation, and analysts say while there’s the risk with an early election, it might be worth striking while the iron’s hot.
We will bring you the details as soon as Sánchez begins his speech.
Elsewhere, up to 500 schools remain closed in France following nationwide protests against classroom conditions last week which also saw outbursts of violence and teachers attacked.

blocks.caption: Police officers secure the area as students arrive to attend their classes at the Camille Jullian secondary school in Bordeaux, France. Photograph: Philippe Lopez/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: And Germany – Ukraine’s largest financial backer – says it will not be intimidated by Russian strikes after chancellor Friedrich Merz announced $1.1bn in military aid in his surprise visit to Kyiv yesterday, which was also marked by a drone strike on a city bridge.

blocks.caption: Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy and German chancellor Friedrich Merz in Ukraine over the weekend. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany Bundesregierung/Tobias Koch/Shutterstock

blocks.text: I will bring you all the latest from across Europe here.
It’s Monday, 5 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: Yemen launches major military operation against Houthis
articles.summary: Yemen's internationally recognized government announced a new military offensive to retake Houthi-held territory after rebels cut a key road linking the city of Taiz with Aden.

image.caption: The recent Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the besieged city of Taiz [September 22, 2014]Image: Mohammed Hamoud/Anadolu Agency/picture alliance

blocks.text: Yemen's Saudi-backed government on Sunday announced a new military operation to retake territory held by Iran-backed Houthi rebels, as fighting intensified around the key southwestern city of Taiz.

"Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory," Yemeni Presidential Council chief Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address.
The announcement came after Houthi fighters captured a key road linking Taiz with the government-held city of Aden, effectively isolating Taiz. The rebels have besieged Taiz for more than a decade.
More than 70 people were reportedly killed in fighting around Taiz over the past day, according to AFP news agency.

blocks.caption: The escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has revived Yemen’s civil war after a four-year ceasefire [FILE: September 27, 2026]Image: Social Media/REUTERS

blocks.text: How did the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Houthis escalate?

The latest developments come amid an escalation between the Houthis and the internationally recognized government in Yemen that is supported by Saudi Arabia, reviving Yemen's civil war after a four-year ceasefire.
A 2022 truce between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia collapsed in July after the rebels allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa, which defied the Saudis' control over Yemeni airspace.
As a result of the escalation, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia.

Last month, the Houthis seized Yemen's Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — a vital global shipping route — from government hands, even as Al-Alimi called for support from the international community.
The Houthis have controlled Sanaa and much of Yemen's more populous western areas since the start of Yemen's civil war in 2014.
Why can't the Saudis defeat the Houthis?

articles.title: Hundreds of French schools shut, teen loses hand in protests
articles.summary: The student protests that rocked France last week have prompted authorities to keep up to 500 schools closed on Monday. A teenage boy lost his hand, seemingly while trying to pick up a police tear…
